Incorporating EBV DNA surveillance into follow-up is a standard component of post-treatment management, making option E correct.

Maintenance immune checkpoint inhibitors are not currently supported by evidence in non-metastatic NPC. Trials evaluating such strategies are ongoing, but routine use outside of clinical trials is not recommended. There is no indication for maintenance immunotherapy after curative-intent chemoradiotherapy in this setting, rendering option F incorrect and potentially exposing the patient to unnecessary toxicity.

A 74-year-old man with metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer (mCRPC) presents with radiographic progression after 14 months of enzalutamide therapy. He is asymptomatic with an ECOG performance status of 0. Ga-68 PSMA-11 PET/CT reveals new PSMA-positive bone metastases without any PSMA-negative lesions. He has not received any chemotherapy for his mCRPC. His prior treatment included docetaxel during the castration-sensitive phase of his disease, completed 18 months ago. He expresses a strong preference to avoid cytotoxic chemotherapy at this time. Laboratory studies show a PSA of 18.4 ng/mL, hemoglobin 13.8 g/dL, and normal renal function. He is currently receiving zoledronic acid every 12 weeks for skeletal protection. Given his PSMA-avid disease and clinical course, what are the most appropriate next steps in management? The patient is being evaluated in a multidisciplinary clinic with access to radiopharmaceutical therapy and advanced radiotherapy techniques.

**Select all that apply:**
A. Initiate Lu-177-PSMA-617 therapy
B. Switch to cabazitaxel chemotherapy
C. Continue current systemic therapy and add metastasis-directed radiotherapy to the new lesions
D. Switch to abiraterone acetate
E. Administer zoledronic acid every 12 weeks
F. Administer zoledronic acid every 3 to 4 weeks

**Answer:** A, C, E

**Rationale:**
The patient has PSMA-positive mCRPC with radiographic progression on enzalutamide, a prior ARPI. He previously received docetaxel in the castration-sensitive setting, but not during the castration-resistant phase. Recent evidence supports the use of Lu-177-PSMA-617 in patients who have progressed on an ARPI and have not yet received taxane chemotherapy in the mCRPC setting, provided they have PSMA-avid disease. The PSMAfore trial demonstrated improved progression-free survival with Lu-177-PSMA-617 compared to an alternative ARPI, establishing it as a standard option in this pre-docetaxel mCRPC population. Therefore, initiating Lu-177-PSMA-617 is appropriate and aligns with current indications.

Continuing enzalutamide and adding metastasis-directed radiotherapy is also a valid option, particularly given the oligoprogressive nature of his disease—limited to new bone lesions on imaging. Trials such as ARTO and GROU-PCS-9 have shown that consolidative radiotherapy to progressing sites while maintaining the current ARPI can delay the need for systemic therapy change and improve progression-free survival. This approach is especially suitable for patients with minimal disease progression and good performance status.

Zoledronic acid every 12 weeks is the preferred dosing schedule for skeletal protection in patients with bone metastases from prostate cancer. Non-inferiority trials have demonstrated that this extended interval maintains efficacy in preventing skeletal-related events while reducing renal toxicity and treatment burden. Administering it every 3 to 4 weeks is outdated and no longer recommended in patients with normal renal function.

Switching to cabazitaxel is not indicated here, as it is typically reserved for patients who have progressed on both an ARPI and a taxane chemotherapy in the mCRPC setting. This patient has not received taxane in the castration-resistant phase, making earlier use of cabazitaxel premature and inconsistent with optimal sequencing.

Switching to abiraterone acetate is not the best choice due to cross-resistance between ARPIs. The CARD trial showed limited efficacy of switching from one ARPI to another, particularly after progression on enzalutamide. Therefore, this approach is inferior to newer options like Lu-177-PSMA-617 in this clinical context.

Administering zoledronic acid every 3 to 4 weeks is no longer standard practice. While historically used, this more frequent schedule has been superseded by the 12-week regimen, which provides equivalent skeletal protection with improved safety and convenience. Continuing the 12-week schedule is appropriate and should not be intensified without indication.

A 62-year-old man presents with a 4-month history of rectal bleeding and altered bowel habits. Colonoscopy reveals a moderately differentiated adenocarcinoma in the mid-rectum. He undergoes a low anterior resection with total mesorectal excision. Pathologic examination shows the primary tumor penetrates the muscularis propria into the perirectal fat but does not reach the visceral peritoneum. In the perirectal fat, a 4 mm discrete tumor nodule is identified, separate from the main tumor mass. Microscopic evaluation reveals a residual rim of lymphoid tissue with a subcapsular sinus within the nodule. All 14 other retrieved lymph nodes are negative for malignancy. The final staging includes this nodule in the N category. Separately, a 55-year-old woman undergoes total mesorectal excision for a low rectal adenocarcinoma. Pathology reveals a pT1 tumor invading the submucosa with 2 of 16 regional lymph nodes positive for metastasis (pT1 N1b). During follow-up, she inquires why her prognosis is considered more favorable than that of a relative who had a pT3 N0 tumor despite her lymph node involvement. The oncology team prepares to counsel her using current prognostic models based on comprehensive staging data.

**Select all that apply:**
A. Classify the 4 mm nodule as a regional lymph node metastasis due to the presence of residual lymphoid tissue and subcapsular sinus
B. Classify the 4 mm nodule as a tumor deposit (N1c) because it is a discrete mass separate from the primary tumor
C. Explain that her favorable prognosis compared to pT3 N0 disease reflects the strong independent prognostic impact of lower T stage, even in the presence of nodal metastases
D. Explain that nodal status is the dominant prognostic factor in rectal cancer, so her pT1 N1b stage carries a worse prognosis than pT3 N0
E. Stage the primary tumor as T3 based on invasion through the muscularis propria into perirectal fat without visceral peritoneal involvement
F. Stage the primary tumor as T4a due to penetration into perirectal fat, regardless of visceral peritoneal contact

**Answer:** A, C, E

**Rationale:**
The presence of lymphoid architecture, including a subcapsular sinus, within a perirectal tumor nodule definitively classifies it as a metastatic regional lymph node rather than a tumor deposit. This histologic criterion is essential for accurate N staging; therefore, classifying the 4 mm nodule as a lymph node metastasis (N1a) is correct. In contrast, classifying it as a tumor deposit (N1c) is incorrect because N1c applies only to nodules lacking lymphoid tissue, which is not the case here. Accurate classification directly impacts staging and treatment planning. The patient’s pT1 N1b status confers a more favorable rectal cancer-specific survival compared to pT3 N0 disease, which is consistent with contemporary data showing that lower T stage, even with nodal involvement, can be associated with better outcomes than higher T stage without nodal spread. This reflects the powerful independent prognostic value of T category in rectal cancer, particularly when comparing Stage IIIA (T1-2, N1) with Stage IIA (T3, N0). Conversely, asserting that nodal status is the dominant prognostic factor misrepresents current evidence in rectal adenocarcinoma, where T stage has been shown to exert a greater influence on survival in specific stage comparisons. T staging is determined by depth of invasion: penetration through the muscularis propria into non-peritonealized perirectal fat defines T3 disease. Staging the tumor as T4a would require invasion through the visceral peritoneum or into adjacent organs, which is not present; thus, T4a classification is incorrect and would overstage the tumor. Overstaging could lead to unnecessary treatment intensification, underscoring the importance of precise pathologic assessment.

A 45-year-old woman presents with an asymptomatic 1.8 cm right thyroid nodule. Fine-needle aspiration cytology reveals a follicular neoplasm (Bethesda IV). Molecular testing is attempted but fails due to nucleic acid degradation. She has no history of radiation exposure, normal vocal cord mobility on ultrasound, and no suspicious lymph nodes. A 62-year-old man is found to have a 0.7 cm papillary thyroid microcarcinoma in the isthmus; high-resolution ultrasound shows the nodule abuts the anterior trachea but without extrathyroidal extension, gross invasion, or abnormal nodes. He strongly prefers to avoid surgery. Separately, a 30-year-old woman underwent total thyroidectomy and central neck dissection for a 3.5 cm papillary carcinoma with nodal micrometastases. She is breastfeeding her 4-month-old infant and requires adjuvant radioactive iodine (I-131) therapy. Her oncologist considers using thyrotropin alfa to prepare her for treatment while ensuring infant safety and optimal therapeutic uptake. The clinical team reviews the indications for thyrotropin alfa, particularly in the context of metastatic disease and lactation-related precautions, to determine the safest and most effective management strategy for these patients. Current evidence supports the use of recombinant human TSH in various clinical settings, including those requiring remnant ablation or treatment of metastatic disease, with attention to proper patient preparation and radiation safety.

**Select all that apply:**
A. Proceed with diagnostic thyroid lobectomy or repeat fine-needle aspiration for the Bethesda IV nodule
B. Initiate active surveillance with serial ultrasound for the follicular neoplasm given inconclusive molecular testing
C. Recommend active surveillance with clinical and sonographic monitoring for the low-risk papillary microcarcinoma
D. Perform definitive total thyroidectomy for the isthmic microcarcinoma due to its proximity to the trachea
E. Discontinue breastfeeding permanently at least 6 to 8 weeks before administering radioactive iodine
F. Administer thyrotropin alfa prior to radioactive iodine therapy to enhance iodine uptake, including in potential metastatic disease

**Answer:** A, C, F

**Rationale:**
For the 45-year-old with a Bethesda IV nodule and failed molecular testing, the risk of malignancy remains substantial at 20–34%. Surveillance without definitive diagnosis is inappropriate in this setting due to the potential for follicular carcinoma. Current guidelines support either diagnostic lobectomy or repeat fine-needle aspiration to obtain adequate tissue for diagnosis, making option A correct. Option B, initiating surveillance for a Bethesda IV lesion with no further diagnostic steps, is not aligned with standard management and increases the risk of delayed cancer treatment, particularly when molecular data is unavailable.

For the 62-year-old with a low-risk papillary microcarcinoma abutting the trachea but without extrathyroidal extension, active surveillance is an established alternative to immediate surgery. Modern guidelines recognize that anatomical proximity alone does not confer high risk, and patient preference for non-surgical management is valid when supported by appropriate monitoring. Thus, option C is correct. In contrast, option D recommends total thyroidectomy based solely on location, which overestimates the risk and disregards current evidence supporting observation in such cases, making it an outdated and unnecessarily aggressive approach.

For the lactating woman requiring I-131 therapy, discontinuation of breastfeeding at least 6 to 8 weeks prior to treatment is essential to allow involution of lactating breast tissue, minimizing radiation exposure to both mother and infant. Option E correctly reflects this safety protocol. However, the use of thyrotropin alfa in this context is not only safe but also indicated, including in patients with distant metastases, as it effectively stimulates iodine uptake without requiring thyroid hormone withdrawal. The belief that thyrotropin alfa is not approved or ineffective in metastatic disease is incorrect; current FDA labeling and clinical guidelines support its use in such settings. Therefore, option F is correct. Failure to use thyrotropin alfa in eligible patients may result in suboptimal preparation and unnecessary morbidity from hypothyroidism.

A 45-year-old woman presents with a 2.5 cm thyroid nodule detected on routine examination. She is euthyroid, asymptomatic, and has no history of radiation exposure or family history of thyroid cancer. Ultrasound reveals a solid nodule with microcalcifications and irregular margins, classified as suspicious. Fine-needle aspiration cytology is performed and reported as atypia of undetermined significance (Bethesda III). Given the indeterminate result, reflex molecular testing is conducted on the FNA specimen, which identifies a BRAF V600E mutation, a genetic alteration strongly associated with papillary thyroid carcinoma. The patient expresses significant anxiety about surgery, particularly concerns about vocal cord paralysis and hypoparathyroidism, and strongly prefers to avoid an operation if possible. She requests a non-surgical management strategy and is agreeable to close monitoring with serial ultrasounds. Concurrently, a 52-year-old man presents with a 2.0 cm hypoechoic, solid right thyroid nodule and a 6-month history of chronic, unexplained diarrhea. FNA yields scant cellular material; the cytopathologist notes a few spindle-shaped cells and reports the findings as 'indeterminate, suspicious for medullary thyroid carcinoma' due to limited sample and atypical morphology. In a separate case, a 38-year-old woman is found to have a 1.8 cm right thyroid nodule on incidental imaging. Ultrasound shows a mildly hypoechoic nodule without microcalcifications, extrathyroidal extension, or abnormal lymph nodes. FNA is diagnostic of follicular neoplasm (Bethesda IV). She is otherwise healthy, with no risk factors for thyroid cancer. Her local hospital does not offer advanced molecular testing. She declines surgery and wishes to pursue observation with periodic imaging.

**Select all that apply:**
A. Active nodule surveillance with serial ultrasound
B. Thyroid lobectomy or total thyroidectomy
C. Molecular testing of the FNA sample
D. Serum calcitonin measurement
E. Serial fine-needle aspiration in 3-6 months
F. Total thyroidectomy with central neck dissection

**Answer:** A, C

**Rationale:**
Active nodule surveillance with serial ultrasound is an appropriate primary management option for the 45-year-old woman with a Bethesda III nodule and a BRAF V600E mutation. Contemporary guidelines support surveillance as a valid alternative to immediate surgery in patients with molecularly high-risk indeterminate nodules when imaging features are not overtly aggressive and the patient expresses a preference to avoid surgery. This approach allows for deferred intervention while maintaining high rates of cancer detection and excellent oncologic outcomes. Similarly, in the 38-year-old woman with a Bethesda IV nodule and no high-risk features, surveillance is a recognized option, particularly when molecular testing is unavailable and the patient declines surgery. Molecular testing of the FNA sample is the most appropriate next step in the 52-year-old man with cytologically indeterminate features suspicious for medullary thyroid carcinoma. Given the limited cellularity and ambiguous morphology, molecular analysis can detect RET mutations or other markers that confirm the diagnosis and guide definitive management. This is preferred over immediate surgery or indirect biochemical testing in this diagnostic context. Thyroid lobectomy or total thyroidectomy, while historically standard for Bethesda III/IV nodules with malignant molecular markers, is no longer considered mandatory in all cases. Current evidence supports shared decision-making and non-surgical management when patient preferences and clinical factors align, making surgery an optional rather than obligatory intervention. Serum calcitonin measurement, though traditionally used in suspected medullary carcinoma, is less specific and sensitive than molecular testing when cytology is indeterminate and may yield false positives in chronic kidney disease or proton pump inhibitor use. It is no longer recommended as the initial diagnostic step in this setting. Serial fine-needle aspiration is not indicated for ongoing monitoring of Bethesda III or IV nodules, as repeat FNA often yields similar indeterminate results and does not reliably exclude malignancy. It delays definitive management without improving diagnostic accuracy. Total thyroidectomy with central neck dissection is excessive as an initial step without confirmed malignancy or lymph node involvement and should only follow a definitive diagnosis of medullary or aggressive papillary carcinoma.

A 56-year-old male presents with newly diagnosed metastatic rectal cancer. Molecular profiling demonstrates a KRAS G12D mutation, BRAF wild-type, and pMMR/MSS status. He has a known history of Gilbert syndrome with mildly elevated baseline serum unconjugated bilirubin. Restaging contrast-enhanced CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis demonstrates multiple bilateral pulmonary metastases and a single 1.2 cm equivocal, indeterminate lesion in the right hepatic lobe. The multidisciplinary tumor board recommends initiating systemic therapy with FOLFIRI plus bevacizumab. Which of the following management steps should be incorporated into this patient's diagnostic and therapeutic plan?

**Select all that apply:**
A. Obtain UGT1A1 testing prior to initiating irinotecan to guide appropriate dose modifications and mitigate the risk of severe neutropenia and diarrhea.
B. Proceed with irinotecan administration using clinical caution without routine molecular screening; although UGT1A1 testing is commercially available, guidelines for its clinical practice use have not been established.
C. Obtain an FDG-PET/CT scan to accurately characterize the equivocal hepatic lesion and assess for potential occult metastatic disease.
D. Monitor the hepatic lesion exclusively with standard contrast-enhanced CT or MRI, as FDG-PET/CT should not be utilized in this setting.
E. Substitute the planned regimen with FOLFOX, as irinotecan is absolutely contraindicated in patients with hyperbilirubinemia and Gilbert syndrome.
F. Add panitumumab to the FOLFIRI regimen instead of bevacizumab to directly target the KRAS G12D mutation and improve systemic response rates.

**Answer:** A, C

**Rationale:**
The management of metastatic rectal cancer requires a multidisciplinary approach integrating molecular profiling, pharmacogenomics, and advanced imaging to tailor therapy to the individual patient. In this case, the patient's genetic status (KRAS G12D, pMMR/MSS) and clinical history (Gilbert syndrome) dictate specific precautions regarding drug selection and toxicity monitoring, while the presence of an equivocal liver lesion necessitates optimal diagnostic clarification.

Pharmacogenomic testing for UGT1A1 polymorphisms is a critical component of safety when utilizing irinotecan-based regimens like FOLFIRI. Patients with Gilbert syndrome often possess the UGT1A1*28 allele, which results in reduced expression of the enzyme responsible for glucuronidating SN-38 (the active metabolite of irinotecan). Failure to identify this deficiency can lead to life-threatening neutropenia and severe diarrhea. While older clinical descriptions may have suggested that routine testing was not standard, modern oncology practice has evolved to recommend UGT1A1 screening as a standard safety measure for high-risk patients to guide initial dose modifications.

Regarding diagnostic imaging, while contrast-enhanced CT and MRI remain the standards for routine monitoring of metastatic disease, FDG-PET/CT serves a specific and vital role in the management of equivocal findings. The identification of a 1.2 cm indeterminate hepatic lesion on CT requires further characterization to determine if it represents a metastatic focus, which could significantly impact the patient's prognosis and potential for future curative-intent metastasectomy. Categorical recommendations against PET/CT in colorectal cancer are outdated; instead, its selective use to resolve diagnostic ambiguity is endorsed by current clinical evidence to enhance staging accuracy.

Finally, the patient's molecular profile is essential for determining the efficacy of targeted therapies. Since the patient has a KRAS G12D mutation, anti-EGFR therapies such as panitumumab or cetuximab are contraindicated, as these agents only provide benefit in patients with RAS wild-type tumors. For KRAS-mutated disease, anti-angiogenic therapy with bevacizumab remains the preferred biologic addition to first-line chemotherapy. Furthermore, while KRAS G12C-specific inhibitors are emerging for that specific mutation, they are typically used in combination with EGFR inhibitors to overcome resistance and are not indicated for the G12D variant found in this patient.

A 66-year-old woman with a history of metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) and compensated cirrhosis (CTP Class A) presents with weight loss and abdominal pain. Multiphasic MRI shows a 7 cm liver mass with multiple bilateral pulmonary metastases. A core needle biopsy of the liver mass reveals a biphenotypic mixed HCC-CCA. The initial biopsy exhibits predominantly cholangiocarcinoma (CCA) histologic features. Multigene panel testing shows no targetable mutations. She requires systemic therapy. After 6 months of initial treatment, she experiences disease progression. A repeat core needle biopsy of an enlarging liver lesion is performed, demonstrating a shift to predominantly hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) features. She maintains an ECOG performance status of 1 and normal bilirubin. Which of the following strategies represent appropriate systemic management for her initially and upon progression?

**Select all that apply:**
A. For first-line therapy, initiate cisplatin and gemcitabine combined with durvalumab specifically because her initial tumor features were predominantly CCA.
B. For first-line therapy, initiate cisplatin and gemcitabine combined with pembrolizumab because this regimen is a universally recommended standard for all advanced mixed HCC-CCA cases.
C. Upon progression, initiate a regimen of ipilimumab and nivolumab, as this combination is a universally appropriate second-line option for mixed HCC-CCA without targetable aberrations.
D. Upon progression, avoid ipilimumab and nivolumab due to a lack of robust evidence, and instead initiate regorafenib tailored to the newly dominant HCC features.
E. For first-line therapy, initiate atezolizumab and bevacizumab specifically because her initial tumor features were predominantly CCA.
F. Upon progression, initiate FOLFOX to target the initially dominant CCA histology, disregarding the repeat biopsy results.

**Answer:** B, C

**Rationale:**
Mixed hepatocellular-cholangiocarcinoma (HCC-CCA) is a rare primary liver malignancy containing histopathologic features of both HCC and CCA. Historically, systemic management for advanced mixed HCC-CCA was tailored to the dominant histologic component (e.g., using gemcitabine/cisplatin for tumors with predominant CCA features or atezolizumab/bevacizumab for HCC-dominant features). However, current medical understanding has evolved to favor a 'universal' approach. This transition acknowledges the biphenotypic nature of these tumors, where both components contribute to disease progression. Consequently, regimens with activity against both histologies are now prioritized over histology-specific tailoring.

For first-line therapy, the current standard is a combination of cisplatin and gemcitabine with an immune checkpoint inhibitor—specifically either durvalumab or pembrolizumab. This regimen is appropriate for all advanced mixed HCC-CCA cases because it integrates the standard of care for biliary tract cancers (gemcitabine/cisplatin/durvalumab or pembrolizumab) with agents that also possess anti-tumor activity in HCC. This universal approach replaces the older strategy of selecting therapy based on which histology appears more prominent on the initial core needle biopsy.

Upon disease progression, management should involve a repeat biopsy to reassess the dominant histology and multigene panel testing (MGPT) to identify targetable alterations common in CCA (such as FGFR2 or IDH1). In the absence of targetable alterations, the management shift continues to emphasize universal regimens over tailored ones. The combination of ipilimumab and nivolumab, along with regorafenib, are now considered reasonable second-line options. This represents a significant change from previous paradigms where dual-immunotherapy was often avoided in mixed tumors due to a perceived lack of robust clinical evidence. The current recommendation to include ipilimumab and nivolumab as a universal second-line option reflects the ongoing integration of established HCC and CCA therapies into unified management protocols for mixed tumors.

A 64-year-old female with metastatic nonsquamous NSCLC has experienced disease progression following 6 cycles of carboplatin, pemetrexed, and pembrolizumab, followed by maintenance pemetrexed and pembrolizumab. Biomarker profiling of a recent biopsy reveals an absence of actionable driver mutations (EGFR, ALK, ROS1 wild-type) but demonstrates HER2 protein overexpression (IHC 3+). The patient is asymptomatic with an ECOG performance status of 0. The oncologist plans to initiate fam-trastuzumab deruxtecan-nxki under its FDA accelerated approval for HER2-positive (IHC 3+) solid tumors. During peer-to-peer review with the insurance medical director, the oncologist must cite the clinical trials forming the basis of this tumor-agnostic indication to justify coverage. Which of the following statements accurately reflects the trial data validating this regimen for this patient's presentation?

**Select all that apply:**
A. The FDA's tumor-agnostic approval necessitates evidence of an activating ERBB2 (HER2) mutation, not merely IHC 3+ protein overexpression.
B. The justification for extending this pan-tumor approval to the patient's NSCLC relies strictly on the phase 2 single-arm DESTINY-Lung01 trial.
C. The broad pan-tumor accelerated approval for this indication is primarily anchored by the DESTINY-PanTumor02 trial.
D. The DESTINY-Lung01 and DESTINY-CRC02 trials function as supporting cohort data alongside the primary pan-tumor trial, rather than the sole anchors.
E. The applicability to NSCLC under this specific HER2 accelerated approval is derived entirely from the response rates of the DESTINY-Lung01 trial.
F. The patient must have an HGF receptor (c-Met) overexpression ≥50% to qualify for this tumor-agnostic approval.

**Answer:** C, D

**Rationale:**
The accelerated approval of fam-trastuzumab deruxtecan-nxki for patients with unresectable or metastatic HER2-positive (IHC 3+) solid tumors marks a significant transition toward biomarker-driven, tumor-agnostic oncology. This approval is specifically predicated on protein overexpression, as determined by immunohistochemistry (IHC 3+), rather than the presence of specific activating ERBB2 (HER2) mutations. Clinicians must recognize that this regulatory pathway allows for the use of the agent in diverse histologies where HER2 protein is highly expressed, provided the patient meets the specified IHC criteria. It is essential to differentiate this pan-tumor approval from earlier, disease-specific indications.

Option C is correct because the pivotal regulatory foundation for the broad, tumor-agnostic accelerated approval is the DESTINY-PanTumor02 trial. This trial provided the necessary efficacy and safety data across multiple diverse solid tumor types to support the FDA decision. Option D is correct because, while trials such as DESTINY-Lung01 (for NSCLC) and DESTINY-CRC02 (for colorectal cancer) were instrumental in demonstrating the drug's activity in specific disease settings, they are viewed within the regulatory framework as supporting cohorts that substantiate the overarching pan-tumor efficacy observed in the broader clinical development program, rather than acting as the sole, exclusive anchors for the pan-tumor indication.

Option A is incorrect because the eligibility criteria for this specific accelerated approval are defined by protein overexpression (IHC 3+), not genomic sequencing for ERBB2 mutations. Options B and E are incorrect because they rely on an incomplete interpretation of the regulatory data. While DESTINY-Lung01 provided critical evidence regarding the activity of fam-trastuzumab deruxtecan-nxki in HER2-overexpressing NSCLC, it is not the sole clinical trial anchoring the pan-tumor indication. Relying exclusively on this single cohort is insufficient to explain the broad regulatory scope. Finally, Option F is incorrect as it conflates distinct therapeutic biomarkers; HGF receptor (c-Met) overexpression is the target for telisotuzumab vedotin, which requires a completely different biomarker assessment profile.

A 52-year-old male presents for management of a 4.2 cm thyroid nodule. Fine-needle aspiration (FNA) was reported as a 'follicular neoplasm, oncocytic (Hürthle cell) type.' He undergoes a total thyroidectomy. Permanent histology reveals a solitary encapsulated mass with oncocytic cells and evidence of 5 foci of vascular invasion. Postoperative staging workup including a chest CT identifies multiple bilateral pulmonary nodules, which are confirmed to be metastatic thyroid cancer on biopsy. The physician is determining the formal diagnosis and staging for this patient according to the latest clinical standards.

**Select all that apply:**
A. Formally classify the malignancy as 'Oncocytic carcinoma,' recognizing it as a distinct clinical entity rather than a follicular variant.
B. Classify the malignancy as 'Hürthle cell variant of follicular thyroid carcinoma' based on its histologic pattern.
C. Assign the patient to AJCC Stage II based on the presence of distant metastases in a patient under the age of 55.
D. Assign the patient to AJCC Stage I because all patients below the prognostic age threshold with distant metastases are categorized as such.
E. Utilize an age cutoff of 55 years to risk-stratify the patient's mortality risk and determine the AJCC stage.
F. Utilize an age cutoff of 40 or 45 years to determine high-risk status according to established prognostic scoring systems like AMES or AGES.

**Answer:** A, C, E

**Rationale:**
The management and classification of thyroid malignancies have undergone significant changes to better align with the molecular and prognostic characteristics of the disease. For this 52-year-old patient, the formal diagnosis is oncocytic carcinoma, and the stage is determined using the current age threshold of 55 years. Since the patient is 52 and has distant metastases to the lungs, he is classified as Stage II according to the AJCC 8th edition. This case highlights the clinical shift in both nomenclature and prognostic assessment.

Oncocytic carcinoma, formerly known as Hürthle cell carcinoma, was traditionally classified as a variant of follicular thyroid carcinoma. However, contemporary oncology recognizes it as a distinct malignancy. This change, formalized in recent WHO and AJCC updates, is based on the identification of unique somatic mutations in pathways such as RAS/RAF/MAPK and PIK/AKT/MTOR, along with characteristic mitochondrial DNA variations and copy number alterations. Unlike follicular carcinoma, oncocytic carcinoma tends to be more aggressive and has a higher propensity for distant metastasis. Diagnosis cannot be confirmed via Fine-Needle Aspiration (FNA) or frozen section alone, as these cannot distinguish between a benign oncocytic adenoma and a carcinoma; postoperative histology showing capsular or vascular invasion (as seen in this patient with 5 foci of vascular invasion) is required for a definitive diagnosis.

Regarding staging, the clinical standard for the age threshold has evolved. While earlier prognostic systems such as AMES, AGES, and previous AJCC editions utilized an age cutoff of 40 or 45 years, the AJCC 8th edition increased this threshold to 55 years. This adjustment was made because data consistently showed that patients under 55 have an exceptionally low mortality risk, even when regional lymph node metastases or other traditionally high-risk features are present. 

Furthermore, the staging for patients under this age threshold has become more granular. Previously, all patients below the age cutoff were grouped into Stage I regardless of whether distant metastases (M1) were present. The current staging system now differentiates between localized disease (Stage I) and distant metastatic disease (Stage II) for patients under 55. This change ensures that the presence of distant metastases, which remains a principal cause of death in differentiated thyroid cancers, is appropriately reflected in the patient's stage and subsequent management plan. While the mortality risk in this group remains lower than in older cohorts, Stage II status correctly identifies a population that requires more intensive surveillance and potential systemic or radioactive iodine therapy.

A 72-year-old man presents with early satiety, fatigue, and left upper quadrant fullness. Physical examination reveals massive splenomegaly extending 12 cm below the costal margin, without lymphadenopathy. Laboratory studies show hemoglobin of 9.2 g/dL, platelet count of 85,000/μL, and normal white blood cell count. Bone marrow biopsy and peripheral blood flow cytometry confirm splenic marginal zone lymphoma (SMZL). Hepatitis C serology is negative. The patient is symptomatic and requires treatment initiation. He has no significant comorbidities and prefers non-surgical management. Concurrently, a 65-year-old woman with nodal marginal zone lymphoma presents after relapse 2 years following complete response to bendamustine and rituximab. She now has symptomatic adenopathy and strongly prefers oral therapy. She inquires about ibrutinib, having read about it online. She has no history of cardiovascular disease or arrhythmias. Molecular profiling confirms BTK pathway activation. Both patients are evaluated in the same clinic session, and treatment decisions must be made based on current evidence-based standards.

**Select all that apply:**
A. Initiate rituximab monotherapy as the preferred standard intervention for the 72-year-old man with SMZL.
B. Proceed with splenectomy as the primary intervention for the 72-year-old man due to presumed lack of response to rituximab.
C. Prescribe zanubrutinib to the 65-year-old woman with relapsed nodal MZL, counseling that ibrutinib is no longer recommended due to lack of confirmed clinical benefit and safety concerns.
D. Prescribe ibrutinib monotherapy to the 65-year-old woman as a valid, retained treatment option for relapsed MZL.
E. Discuss that rituximab-based therapy is the standard first-line approach for SMZL, supporting the use of rituximab in the 72-year-old man.
F. Administer bendamustine plus obinutuzumab as the only potentially curative regimen for the 72-year-old man with SMZL.

**Answer:** A, C, E

**Rationale:**
Rituximab monotherapy is the established standard first-line treatment for symptomatic splenic marginal zone lymphoma. It induces high rates of hematologic recovery and splenic response with minimal toxicity, making it preferred over splenectomy, which carries surgical risks and long-term infection concerns. Current guidelines strongly support rituximab as initial therapy, reserving splenectomy for rituximab-refractory cases or specific contraindications. Option A correctly reflects this standard, emphasizing rituximab as the preferred intervention. Option E reinforces this by affirming the centrality of rituximab in frontline management, aligning with consensus recommendations. In contrast, option B promotes splenectomy as primary therapy based on the outdated notion that SMZL is unresponsive to rituximab, which is no longer valid; this approach is no longer recommended as initial care. For relapsed nodal MZL, covalent BTK inhibitors like zanubrutinib are preferred oral agents. Zanubrutinib has demonstrated efficacy and a favorable safety profile, leading to its endorsement in current algorithms. Option C correctly selects zanubrutinib and includes appropriate counseling about ibrutinib’s regulatory withdrawal. Ibrutinib initially received accelerated approval but failed to confirm clinical benefit in follow-up trials and was withdrawn from the MZL indication due to lack of survival advantage and fatal adverse events. Thus, option D is incorrect despite historical use, as it no longer represents standard care. Option F is incorrect because bendamustine plus obinutuzumab is not considered curative in SMZL and is not a first-line standard for this subtype; its use is more relevant in other B-cell lymphomas. Pirtobrutinib is not mentioned as it is reserved for post-covalent BTK inhibitor progression and was not part of the correct clinical decisions for these cases.

A 35-year-old woman presents with headaches, gait instability, and mild nausea over the past three weeks. Neurological examination reveals mild truncal ataxia but no cranial nerve deficits or long tract signs. MRI of the brain demonstrates a well-circumscribed, homogeneously enhancing mass in the cerebellar vermis with restricted diffusion and no surrounding edema. There is mild obstructive hydrocephalus. She undergoes gross total resection without complications. Histopathology confirms medulloblastoma, classic variant. Molecular profiling reveals a somatic CTNNB1 mutation, confirming WNT pathway activation. Staging evaluation, including MRI of the entire neuroaxis and lumbar puncture for cerebrospinal fluid cytology, shows no evidence of leptomeningeal dissemination. Post-operatively, she has made an excellent recovery with resolution of her symptoms and no residual neurological deficits. During her follow-up visit, she inquires about her long-term prognosis and what the molecular results mean for her outcome. She is particularly concerned about the likelihood of recurrence and overall survival. Additionally, the oncology team discusses the next steps in adjuvant therapy, weighing the risks and benefits of radiation and chemotherapy in light of her tumor biology and disease status.

**Select all that apply:**
A. Proceed with adjuvant craniospinal irradiation followed by boost to the tumor bed as standard of care regardless of molecular subtype
B. Counsel the patient that her tumor subtype is associated with an excellent long-term survival and low risk of recurrence
C. Counsel the patient that her tumor's molecular profile is linked to a less favorable prognosis based on adult-specific data
D. Defer adjuvant radiotherapy and recommend close observation with serial neuroimaging given the molecular and clinical context
E. Initiate high-dose chemotherapy with stem cell rescue as the primary adjuvant strategy
F. Administer focal radiotherapy alone, avoiding craniospinal irradiation due to lower risk of spinal seeding

**Answer:** C, D

**Rationale:**
In adult medulloblastoma, molecular classification has significant prognostic implications, but these differ from pediatric patterns. The presence of a CTNNB1 mutation indicates WNT pathway activation, which in children is strongly associated with exceptional outcomes and low recurrence risk. However, recent adult-specific studies, including a cohort analysis of 28 adult patients, demonstrate that WNT-activated tumors in adults do not share the same favorable prognosis and may instead be linked to poorer survival outcomes. This divergence underscores the importance of age-specific prognostic models and cautions against extrapolating pediatric data to adult patients. Therefore, counseling the patient that her tumor confers excellent survival (Option B) reflects an outdated understanding based solely on pediatric evidence and is not supported by adult data. In contrast, advising that the molecular profile is associated with a less favorable prognosis (Option C) aligns with current adult-specific evidence and provides a more accurate expectation. Regarding adjuvant therapy, while craniospinal irradiation (CSI) has traditionally been the standard for medulloblastoma, adult patients with WNT-activated tumors may not derive the same benefit, and given the potential long-term toxicities of CSI, especially neurocognitive and endocrine effects, deferring radiotherapy in favor of close observation is increasingly considered in select low-risk adults. Option D is therefore appropriate, particularly in the context of gross total resection and negative staging, as it reflects a risk-adapted, evidence-based approach. Option A, recommending routine CSI regardless of subtype, represents a one-size-fits-all strategy that does not incorporate modern molecular risk stratification and exposes the patient to unnecessary toxicity without proven benefit in this subgroup. Option F, using focal radiotherapy alone, is not standard for medulloblastoma due to the risk of spinal dissemination, even in molecularly defined subgroups, and lacks sufficient evidence to replace craniospinal approaches when radiation is indicated. Option E, high-dose chemotherapy with stem cell rescue, is typically reserved for high-risk or recurrent disease and is not indicated as primary adjuvant therapy in a patient with localized disease and no residual tumor, making it an overly aggressive and inappropriate choice in this setting.

A 50-year-old woman with metastatic HER2-negative breast cancer presents with new-onset seizures and progressive cognitive decline over the past two weeks. She has no focal neurological deficits but is increasingly disoriented. Brain MRI with contrast reveals five enhancing lesions within the cerebral parenchyma, ranging from 1.2 to 2.8 cm, consistent with parenchymal brain metastases. There is no hydrocephalus, leptomeningeal enhancement, or spinal involvement. Her performance status is ECOG 1, and systemic disease is stable on current chemotherapy. A multidisciplinary team discusses local therapy options. Separately, a 58-year-old man with metastatic non-small cell lung cancer presents with diplopia, facial numbness, and radicular leg pain. Craniospinal MRI demonstrates diffuse linear enhancement along the brainstem, cerebellar surfaces, and cauda equina, highly suggestive of leptomeningeal disease. Two prior lumbar punctures showed negative cytology, but clinical and radiological findings remain strongly supportive. He is symptomatic and requires immediate intervention. The team considers diagnostic and therapeutic strategies. Additionally, a 62-year-old man with multiple myeloma presents with severe mid-back pain worsened by movement. Spine MRI shows a lytic lesion at T9 with retropulsion of bone fragments into the spinal canal and early spinal cord compression; however, motor strength and sensation are preserved. Structural instability is evident. Finally, a 68-year-old man with metastatic prostate cancer reports persistent lower back pain. MRI reveals a solitary L3 vertebral body metastasis without spinal cord compression, fracture, or instability. He desires rapid pain relief with minimal treatment burden.

**Select all that apply:**
A. Administer intrathecal methotrexate
B. Administer whole-brain radiotherapy
C. Proceed with decompressive spinal surgery and stabilization
D. Administer fractionated external beam radiotherapy (20 Gy in 5 fractions)
E. Administer single-fraction external beam radiotherapy (8 Gy in 1 fraction)
F. Initiate targeted leptomeningeal therapy based on combined clinical and radiological findings

**Answer:** B, C, E, F

**Rationale:**
Whole-brain radiotherapy (Option B) is the standard of care for patients with multiple parenchymal brain metastases, particularly when systemic disease is controlled and performance status is preserved. Radiation effectively targets both visible lesions and microscopic disease within the brain parenchyma. Intrathecal chemotherapy (Option A) does not achieve therapeutic concentrations in the brain tissue due to poor penetration across the pial-glial barrier and is therefore ineffective for parenchymal metastases, despite historical misconceptions about its utility in this setting. Its use should be restricted to leptomeningeal disease. For the patient with multiple myeloma and spinal structural instability with retropulsed bone fragments, decompressive surgery and stabilization (Option C) is the most appropriate intervention. Although hematologic malignancies are often radiosensitive, mechanical compromise of the spinal column requires surgical correction to prevent cord injury and restore stability, a principle supported by modern spinal oncology guidelines. Fractionated radiotherapy (Option D) is appropriate in cases of spinal cord compression when surgery is not feasible or as adjuvant treatment, but it does not address mechanical instability and is not the primary intervention when surgical decompression is indicated. Single-fraction radiotherapy (8 Gy in 1 fraction, Option E) is strongly supported for palliation of pain in patients with isolated spinal metastases without cord compression or instability. Multiple randomized trials confirm equivalent pain relief compared to multifraction regimens with improved convenience and reduced burden. Initiating targeted leptomeningeal therapy based on clinical and radiological findings (Option F) is appropriate when cytology is negative but imaging and symptoms are highly suggestive. Waiting for positive cytology through repeated lumbar punctures risks treatment delays, and current diagnostic criteria allow for clinical-radiological diagnosis. The notion that repeated lumbar punctures reliably achieve 90% sensitivity is overstated; in practice, sensitivity plateaus well below this level, making empiric treatment reasonable in symptomatic patients with strong imaging evidence.

A 45-year-old man with a confirmed germline MSH2 mutation (Lynch syndrome) presents to the survivorship clinic for follow-up three years after undergoing a segmental colectomy for stage I colon adenocarcinoma. Since his surgery, he has undergone annual surveillance colonoscopies, all of which have shown no evidence of recurrent cancer or new polyps. He reports persistent anxiety and significant psychological distress related to the bowel preparation required for these procedures, particularly the volume and taste of polyethylene glycol solution. He tolerates the endoscopic procedures well and has no complications, but he expresses concern about the long-term burden of yearly colonoscopies and asks whether the interval can be safely extended. His family history is notable for colorectal cancer in his father at age 48 and endometrial cancer in his aunt at age 52. He has no personal history of other Lynch-associated malignancies. He is otherwise healthy, takes no medications, and has no signs or symptoms of gastrointestinal disease. Physical examination is unremarkable. He is adherent to annual dermatologic and urologic screening for other Lynch-related cancers. The care team discusses the optimal strategy for ongoing colorectal surveillance, balancing cancer risk, procedural burden, and patient preferences.

**Select all that apply:**
A. Advise taking aspirin 81 mg daily
B. Advise taking aspirin 325 mg daily
C. Schedule the next surveillance colonoscopy in 6 months
D. Schedule the next surveillance colonoscopy in exactly 1 year
E. Schedule the next surveillance colonoscopy at an individualized 1- to 2-year interval
F. Schedule the next surveillance colonoscopy in 3 years

**Answer:** A, E

**Rationale:**
Patients with Lynch syndrome have a markedly increased lifetime risk of colorectal cancer due to defective DNA mismatch repair, and their adenomas can progress to carcinoma more rapidly than in the general population. For this reason, endoscopic surveillance is a cornerstone of management. While annual colonoscopy has historically been the standard, current guidelines support an individualized interval of 1 to 2 years based on the specific gene mutation, prior polyp burden, and patient factors such as psychological distress or procedural tolerance. The MSH2 mutation confers a high risk, but the absence of recurrent lesions over three years and the patient's significant discomfort with bowel preparation justify a tailored approach, making an individualized 1- to 2-year interval appropriate. This balances cancer detection with quality of life and aligns with contemporary recommendations.

Low-dose aspirin (81 mg daily) is supported by evidence for chemoprevention in high-risk individuals, including those with Lynch syndrome. The CAPP2 trial demonstrated a significant reduction in colorectal cancer incidence among Lynch syndrome carriers who received aspirin, with maximal benefit observed after at least two years of use. The 81 mg dose is preferred over higher doses due to comparable efficacy and a more favorable safety profile, particularly regarding gastrointestinal bleeding. Therefore, initiating low-dose aspirin is a reasonable preventive measure in this patient.

Scheduling colonoscopy in 6 months is overly frequent and not supported by guidelines. There is no evidence that surveillance more frequent than annual provides additional benefit, and given the patient's distress, such an interval would exacerbate burden without clinical justification. A fixed annual schedule, while historically common, does not account for individual risk stratification or patient-centered considerations. Although annual surveillance may still be appropriate in some high-risk cases, the flexibility to extend to 2 years when no lesions are found allows for personalized care and is now the standard.

A 3-year interval is inappropriate for any patient with Lynch syndrome, regardless of prior findings. Even in the lowest-risk subtypes (e.g., PMS2), surveillance is not extended beyond 2 years, and for MSH2 carriers, the risk remains substantial. Such a long interval increases the likelihood of missing rapidly developing cancers and contradicts established guidelines. High-dose aspirin (325 mg) is not recommended for chemoprevention in this context due to increased risk of adverse effects without superior efficacy. The lower dose is equally effective and safer, making 325 mg an unnecessary and potentially harmful choice.

A 70-year-old woman with recurrent, unresectable laryngeal squamous cell carcinoma is scheduled to begin first-line systemic therapy with an anti-PD-1 inhibitor, given her PD-L1 Combined Positive Score of 25. She has a history of severe peripheral vascular disease and longstanding diabetes with bilateral lower extremity ulcers, making peripheral intravenous access extremely difficult. Multiple attempts at IV cannulation have failed in prior outpatient visits, causing significant distress. Her oncologist aims to initiate immunotherapy while minimizing procedural burden and avoiding central line placement. She is otherwise in good condition with an ECOG performance status of 1 and preserved organ function. The treatment team considers alternative routes of administration to ensure timely initiation of therapy. Concurrently, a 58-year-old woman presents with an unresectable recurrent salivary gland mass. Biopsy confirms secretory carcinoma, a tumor subtype known for targetable genomic alterations. The oncology team must determine the optimal strategy for molecular profiling to guide potential targeted therapy. Both cases require decisions on therapy delivery and diagnostic testing that align with current standards of care.

**Select all that apply:**
A. Administer subcutaneous pembrolizumab and berahyaluronidase alfa-pmph
B. Administer intravenous pembrolizumab
C. Order comprehensive multigene panel testing including androgen receptor (AR) and tumor mutational burden (TMB) universally
D. Order targeted biomarker testing selectively guided by specific histologic subtype and clinical context
E. Administer nivolumab and hyaluronidase-nvhy subcutaneous injection
F. Initiate hyperfractionated reirradiation to a total dose of 65 Gy

**Answer:** A, C, E

**Rationale:**
Subcutaneous formulations of anti-PD-1 inhibitors are now established options for patients requiring immunotherapy but facing challenges with intravenous access. Administering subcutaneous pembrolizumab and berahyaluronidase alfa-pmph (Option A) is appropriate in this context, as it is FDA-approved and bioequivalent to intravenous pembrolizumab, with comparable efficacy and safety in approved indications. This route significantly reduces infusion time and avoids complications related to difficult venous access, making it a preferred option for patients with comorbidities affecting vascular integrity. Administering nivolumab and hyaluronidase-nvhy subcutaneous injection (Option E) is also valid, as this formulation is approved as a substitute for intravenous nivolumab in approved cancer types, offering similar pharmacokinetic profiles and clinical outcomes while improving patient convenience. Universal comprehensive multigene panel testing (Option C) is the standard of care for patients with unresectable or recurrent salivary gland carcinomas, including secretory carcinoma. These tumors may harbor actionable fusions such as ETV6-NTRK3, but also alterations in AR, HER2, FGFR, and others; thus, broad genomic profiling increases the likelihood of identifying targetable drivers and eligibility for clinical trials or FDA-approved targeted therapies. In contrast, selectively ordering biomarker testing based on histology (Option D) is outdated, as it risks missing rare but therapeutically relevant alterations that may not be predicted by morphology alone, limiting treatment opportunities. Administering intravenous pembrolizumab (Option B), while effective, imposes unnecessary procedural burden in a patient with documented difficult venous access and no contraindication to subcutaneous administration. Given the availability of an equally effective subcutaneous alternative, persisting with IV infusion does not align with current patient-centered care standards. Initiating hyperfractionated reirradiation to 65 Gy (Option F) is inappropriate in this setting, as the patient is being considered for first-line systemic therapy, and reirradiation carries significant toxicity risks, particularly in previously irradiated head and neck regions, without evidence of local control benefit in the absence of resectable disease or palliative indication. The decision to pursue radiation should be multidisciplinary and reserved for select cases with favorable anatomy and performance status, not as a substitute for systemic treatment in metastatic or unresectable disease.

A 64-year-old female never-smoker presents with a chronic cough and progressive dyspnea. Imaging reveals a right upper lobe mass with bilateral pulmonary nodules and pleural effusions. A biopsy confirms metastatic mucinous adenocarcinoma of the lung. She undergoes comprehensive molecular profiling with a DNA-based next-generation sequencing (NGS) panel that evaluates for common driver mutations including EGFR, ALK, ROS1, BRAF, KRAS, and RET, but no actionable alterations are identified. Given her clinical profile and histology, there is suspicion for a rare oncogenic driver. The oncologist considers the possibility of an NRG1 gene fusion, which has been associated with response to investigational HER2/HER3 bispecific antibodies. Additionally, due to disease progression after first-line platinum-pemetrexed therapy, the team evaluates options for targeted therapy. The patient has no prior testing for MET protein expression or HER2 mutations. The clinical team aims to pursue all guideline-concordant biomarker assessments to identify potential therapeutic targets, particularly those relevant to emerging targeted agents. Which of the following diagnostic steps are most appropriate in this setting to guide targeted therapy selection?

**Select all that apply:**
A. Perform DNA-based Next-Generation Sequencing (NGS)
B. Perform RNA-based Next-Generation Sequencing (NGS)
C. Perform Immunohistochemistry (IHC) using the SP44 clone
D. Perform Immunohistochemistry (IHC) to detect HER2 3+ tumor cell staining
E. Evaluate for ERBB2 (HER2) activating mutations using Next-Generation Sequencing (NGS)
F. Evaluate for MET amplification and MET exon 14 skipping events using Next-Generation Sequencing (NGS)

**Answer:** B, C, E

**Rationale:**
The current standard for molecular profiling in advanced non-small cell lung cancer requires a comprehensive, consolidated approach to biomarker detection, prioritizing methodologies that reliably identify both established and emerging actionable alterations. RNA-based NGS is the preferred method for detecting gene fusions such as NRG1, as DNA-based panels often miss these due to large intronic regions not covered in targeted exonic sequencing. Given the negative DNA-NGS result and the clinical suspicion for an NRG1 fusion, proceeding with RNA-based NGS is essential to capture transcript-level fusion events that may guide enrollment in targeted therapy trials. This approach ensures complete molecular characterization beyond what DNA sequencing alone can provide.

Immunohistochemistry using the SP44 clone is the validated method for assessing MET protein overexpression, which is required for eligibility for certain MET-targeted antibody-drug conjugates. While genomic alterations like MET exon 14 skipping or amplification are detected via NGS or FISH, protein expression must be evaluated separately by IHC. The SP44 clone has been analytically and clinically validated in this context, and a result of 3+ staining in ≥50% of tumor cells defines positivity. Relying on genomic testing alone would not suffice for patient selection for this class of therapy.

Evaluation of ERBB2 (HER2) activating mutations via NGS is necessary to determine eligibility for FDA-approved HER2-targeted therapies in NSCLC. These agents, including specific tyrosine kinase inhibitors and antibody-drug conjugates, have demonstrated efficacy predominantly in patients whose tumors harbor activating mutations in the HER2 tyrosine kinase domain. Protein overexpression by IHC, particularly 3+ staining, is no longer considered a reliable predictive biomarker for these therapies and should not be used to guide treatment decisions. Therefore, sequencing for HER2 mutations is the appropriate step.

While DNA-based NGS is a foundational component of initial molecular testing, it is insufficient alone for detecting certain fusion events like NRG1 and should not be repeated without expanding the modality to include RNA analysis. Immunohistochemistry for HER2 3+ staining reflects an outdated approach to patient selection for HER2-targeted therapy and lacks predictive value in current clinical trials and approvals. Evaluating for MET amplification and exon 14 skipping is relevant for MET kinase inhibitors but does not address eligibility for MET-directed antibody-drug conjugates, which depend on protein expression rather than genomic alterations.

A 61-year-old male with a history of smoking presents with persistent cough and hemoptysis. Imaging reveals a right upper lobe mass and mediastinal lymphadenopathy. Endobronchial ultrasound confirms cT2aN2M0 squamous cell carcinoma with metastasis in station 4R. He receives neoadjuvant platinum-based chemotherapy with partial response and undergoes right upper lobectomy with complete mediastinal lymph node dissection. Final pathology shows R0 resection but residual viable tumor in two 4R and one station 7 lymph node, confirming pN2 disease. He recovers well with ECOG 0. A 67-year-old female former smoker presents with fatigue, weight loss, and pleuritic chest pain. CT shows a 4.5 cm right lower lobe mass and multiple liver lesions. Biopsy confirms metastatic lung adenocarcinoma. Molecular testing is negative for EGFR, ALK, ROS1, BRAF, MET, and RET. PD-L1 tumor proportion score is 5%. She expresses strong interest in immunotherapy and asks whether additional biomarker testing, such as tumor mutational burden (TMB), could better predict treatment response. She has no brain metastases and is otherwise asymptomatic.

**Select all that apply:**
A. Proceed with observation, omitting postoperative radiotherapy (PORT)
B. Administer postoperative radiotherapy (PORT) to the mediastinum
C. Select systemic immunotherapy based on PD-L1 expression, omitting TMB testing
D. Order tumor mutational burden (TMB) testing to determine immunotherapy eligibility
E. Initiate definitive concurrent chemoradiotherapy to a dose of 74 Gy
F. Perform prophylactic cranial irradiation (PCI)

**Answer:** B, C

**Rationale:**
For the first patient with resected pN2 squamous cell carcinoma, adjuvant management must balance locoregional control and survival. While earlier studies raised concerns about PORT due to lack of overall survival benefit and increased toxicity, more recent analyses support its use in high-risk cases. This patient has residual nodal disease in multiple stations after neoadjuvant chemotherapy, placing him at high risk for locoregional recurrence. Current guidelines endorse considering PORT in such scenarios to improve local control, particularly when risk factors like multistation N2 involvement are present. Thus, administering PORT to the mediastinum is appropriate. Observation alone (Option A) may be considered in low-risk pN2 patients, but this patient's pathology does not meet those criteria. Definitive chemoradiotherapy to 74 Gy (Option E) is inappropriate here as the patient has already undergone complete surgical resection; this dose is associated with increased mortality compared to 60 Gy in unresectable disease, as shown in RTOG 0617. Prophylactic cranial irradiation (Option F) has no role in the adjuvant setting for NSCLC outside of small cell histology or specific trial contexts and is not indicated. For the second patient with metastatic adenocarcinoma and PD-L1 TPS of 5%, first-line systemic therapy decisions rely on established biomarkers. PD-L1 expression remains a validated and clinically practical biomarker for guiding immunotherapy use. Although early data from CheckMate 227 suggested TMB might predict improved progression-free survival with nivolumab plus ipilimumab, subsequent overall survival analyses showed benefit regardless of TMB status. Additionally, TMB testing suffers from variability in assay platforms, tissue requirements, and lack of standardized thresholds, limiting its clinical utility. As a result, major guidelines no longer recommend TMB for treatment selection in this setting. Therefore, initiating immunotherapy based on PD-L1 status while forgoing TMB testing (Option C) is the appropriate approach. Ordering TMB testing (Option D) reflects an outdated interpretation of the evidence and is not supported by current standards. Option E is irrelevant in a metastatic, surgically unresectable context with no indication for definitive radiotherapy. Option F has no evidence base in non-small cell lung cancer for brain metastasis prevention and is not standard of care.

A 62-year-old man with a 40-pack-year smoking history presents with a persistent cough and undergoes a right upper lobectomy and mediastinal lymph node dissection for a 4 cm lung adenocarcinoma. Final pathology reveals completely resected disease with negative surgical margins (R0). Three of 15 resected mediastinal lymph nodes are positive for metastatic adenocarcinoma, confirming stage IIIA (N2) disease. The pathologist specifically notes extracapsular extension in one of the involved lymph nodes. Following surgery, the patient recovers well and receives four cycles of adjuvant chemotherapy with cisplatin and pemetrexed without significant complications. He remains asymptomatic with an ECOG performance status of 0. Imaging after chemotherapy shows no evidence of residual or recurrent disease. The multidisciplinary tumor board discusses further management options to reduce the risk of locoregional recurrence. The patient has no contraindications to radiotherapy and expresses a strong preference for aggressive treatment to maximize his chances of cure. Consideration is given to additional locoregional therapy, systemic therapy, or observation. His molecular profile is negative for EGFR, ALK, ROS1, and BRAF alterations, and PD-L1 expression is 30%. Given his high-risk pathologic features, the oncology team evaluates the role of postoperative interventions to improve outcomes.

**Select all that apply:**
A. Clinical observation with routine surveillance imaging
B. Postoperative radiotherapy to the mediastinum
C. Consolidation durvalumab
D. Additional cycles of cytotoxic chemotherapy
E. First-line therapy with carboplatin and pemetrexed
F. First-line therapy with sotorasib

**Answer:** B

**Rationale:**
Option A (Clinical observation with routine surveillance imaging) is not the most appropriate choice in this case. Although observation may have been considered in the past for completely resected N2 disease, the presence of extracapsular extension constitutes a high-risk feature that significantly increases the likelihood of locoregional recurrence. Modern evidence supports the use of postoperative radiotherapy in such high-risk R0-resected patients to improve locoregional control, making observation insufficient despite complete resection and adjuvant chemotherapy. Option B (Postoperative radiotherapy to the mediastinum) is the correct approach. Current data support PORT in patients with completely resected stage IIIA N2 NSCLC who have high-risk features such as extracapsular extension, even after adjuvant chemotherapy. This strategy is associated with improved locoregional control without prohibitive toxicity when delivered after chemotherapy, and it aligns with contemporary management for anatomically complex nodal disease. Option C (Consolidation durvalumab) is not indicated in the postoperative setting after adjuvant chemotherapy. Durvalumab is established as consolidation therapy after definitive chemoradiotherapy for unresectable stage III disease, not after surgical resection and adjuvant chemotherapy. There is no evidence supporting its use in resected NSCLC, and it is not part of current adjuvant protocols. Option D (Additional cycles of cytotoxic chemotherapy) is inappropriate. The standard adjuvant regimen consists of four cycles of platinum-based chemotherapy. Extending treatment beyond this duration has not been shown to improve outcomes and increases the risk of cumulative toxicity, including neuropathy and myelosuppression, without survival benefit. Option E (First-line therapy with carboplatin and pemetrexed) refers to initial systemic treatment for advanced disease, not adjuvant or consolidation therapy in the resected setting. This patient has already completed adjuvant chemotherapy, and repeating or initiating 'first-line' therapy is a misapplication of treatment sequencing. Option F (First-line therapy with sotorasib) is incorrect. Sotorasib is a KRAS G12C inhibitor used in the second-line or later setting for metastatic NSCLC with this specific mutation. This patient does not have a KRAS mutation, and even if he did, targeted therapy has no role in the adjuvant or postoperative setting outside of clinical trials.

A 70-year-old female presents with newly diagnosed metastatic lung adenocarcinoma. She is a former smoker with an ECOG performance status of 1 and reports mild fatigue but no significant weight loss or respiratory symptoms. Molecular testing reveals no actionable driver mutations (EGFR, ALK, ROS1 negative), and PD-L1 expression is 0% by immunohistochemistry. She has normal renal, hepatic, and bone marrow function. Given her anxiety about severe chemotherapy side effects—particularly nausea, neuropathy, and kidney toxicity—she expresses a strong preference for a regimen perceived as less toxic, though she remains committed to systemic treatment for disease control. She is not a candidate for immune checkpoint inhibitors due to low PD-L1 expression and absence of tumor mutational burden elevation. The oncology team discusses first-line chemotherapy options with her, emphasizing efficacy, safety, and quality of life. In parallel, a 68-year-old male with metastatic nonsquamous NSCLC completed 6 cycles of carboplatin and pemetrexed with partial response on restaging CT. He has grade 1 fatigue, no neuropathy, and preserved organ function. His oncologist considers next steps. Additionally, a 72-year-old male with advanced squamous cell carcinoma received 4 cycles of cisplatin and gemcitabine with stable disease. Due to severe rheumatoid arthritis on chronic immunosuppression, he cannot receive immunotherapy. He remains asymptomatic with ECOG 1. The treatment team evaluates whether to continue active therapy or transition to surveillance.

**Select all that apply:**
A. Administer gemcitabine and docetaxel
B. Administer cisplatin, gemcitabine, and bevacizumab
C. Discontinue carboplatin and initiate maintenance pemetrexed
D. Continue carboplatin and pemetrexed for an additional 2 cycles (total 8 cycles)
E. Observe with regular follow-up imaging
F. Initiate continuation maintenance with docetaxel

**Answer:** A, C, E

**Rationale:**
For the patient with newly diagnosed metastatic adenocarcinoma concerned about toxicity, gemcitabine plus docetaxel is an appropriate first-line option. Although platinum-based doublets remain the most effective regimens, non-platinum combinations such as gemcitabine and docetaxel have demonstrated clinically meaningful activity and a more favorable toxicity profile, particularly avoiding nephrotoxicity and severe emesis associated with cisplatin. These regimens are considered reasonable alternatives for patients who are not candidates for or express strong aversion to platinum agents, offering palliative benefit and disease control with improved tolerability. Administering cisplatin, gemcitabine, and bevacizumab is incorrect due to histology and safety concerns; bevacizumab is contraindicated in squamous cell carcinoma because of the elevated risk of life-threatening pulmonary hemorrhage, and this patient has adenocarcinoma but no indication for triplet therapy, which adds toxicity without proven survival benefit in this context. Discontinuing carboplatin and initiating maintenance pemetrexed is the standard of care for nonsquamous NSCLC after platinum-based induction, as continuation maintenance with pemetrexed significantly improves overall survival compared to placebo or observation, even in patients with partial response. Continuing carboplatin beyond 6 cycles is not recommended, as it increases cumulative hematologic and renal toxicity without evidence of improved outcomes; modern guidelines cap platinum therapy at 4–6 cycles to optimize the risk-benefit ratio. Observation with regular imaging is the preferred approach after induction chemotherapy in squamous cell carcinoma when no maintenance option has proven survival benefit; trials evaluating gemcitabine or docetaxel maintenance showed minimal progression-free survival gains without overall survival improvement, and in the absence of immunotherapy eligibility, surveillance is favored to avoid unnecessary toxicity. Initiating docetaxel maintenance is not supported in this setting, as no trial has demonstrated a survival advantage for taxane continuation in squamous histology, and it exposes the patient to risks of myelosuppression, fluid retention, and neuropathy without meaningful benefit.

A 62-year-old man presents with newly diagnosed high-risk localized prostate cancer (Gleason 4+5=9, PSA 18 ng/mL, clinical stage T3aN0M0) and undergoes definitive local therapy. Genomic testing reveals a pathogenic germline BRCA2 mutation. He has no personal or family history of breast, ovarian, pancreatic, or melanoma cancers. Given his high-risk features and genetic finding, the oncology team discusses prognosis and surveillance strategy. Separately, a 71-year-old man with metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer (mCRPC) progresses after docetaxel and enzalutamide. A biopsy of a bone lesion confirms typical acinar adenocarcinoma without neuroendocrine or aggressive variant features. The team considers systemic therapy with cabazitaxel and carboplatin. Additionally, a 68-year-old man is diagnosed with de novo metastatic castration-sensitive prostate cancer (mCSPC) with multiple bone metastases. He lacks any personal or family history of prostate, breast, ovarian, pancreatic, or melanoma cancers. The treatment team evaluates whether germline genetic testing is warranted before initiating systemic therapy. These cases collectively prompt a discussion on the prognostic value of DNA repair defects in localized disease, appropriate use of platinum-based chemotherapy in mCRPC, and indications for germline testing in metastatic prostate cancer.

**Select all that apply:**
A. DNA repair defects carry a worse prognosis in metastatic disease but do not appear to be prognostic in localized disease.
B. Germline homologous recombination repair mutations are associated with aggressive pathologic features and an inferior prognosis in localized disease.
C. Germline testing should be guided strictly by clinical presentation and a thorough review of personal and family history of cancer.
D. Universal germline testing for homologous recombination repair mutations is indicated regardless of family cancer history.
E. Cabazitaxel combined with carboplatin is specifically reserved for patients with aggressive variant or neuroendocrine prostate cancer.
F. Primary androgen deprivation therapy (ADT) is a curative monotherapy option for clinically localized N0, M0 disease.

**Answer:** B, D, E

**Rationale:**
In high-risk localized prostate cancer, the presence of a germline BRCA2 mutation is associated with more aggressive tumor biology, including higher Gleason scores, increased risk of extraprostatic extension, and elevated rates of biochemical recurrence and metastasis. Option B is correct because multiple studies, including those from large genomic cohorts, have consistently demonstrated that homologous recombination repair (HRR) mutations confer a worse prognosis even in non-metastatic disease, supporting intensified surveillance and consideration of adjuvant strategies. Option A is incorrect; while DNA repair defects are clearly prognostic in metastatic prostate cancer, emerging evidence refutes the notion that they lack prognostic value in localized disease—this view reflects an outdated understanding no longer supported by contemporary data. Option C is incorrect because restricting germline testing to patients with suggestive personal or family histories fails to identify a substantial proportion of mutation carriers. Current guidelines recommend universal germline testing for all men with metastatic prostate cancer, as up to 50% of those with pathogenic mutations lack a significant family history. Option D is correct, aligning with guideline-endorsed practice that ensures access to targeted therapies such as PARP inhibitors and facilitates cascade testing for at-risk relatives. For metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer, cabazitaxel monotherapy remains a standard option after docetaxel. The addition of carboplatin is not routinely recommended for typical acinar adenocarcinoma due to lack of survival benefit and increased hematologic toxicity. Option E is correct because platinum-based combinations are reserved for patients with aggressive variant prostate cancer or neuroendocrine differentiation, where these regimens show greater activity. Option F is incorrect because primary androgen deprivation therapy alone is not curative for localized disease; definitive local treatment with surgery or radiation is required for cure-intent management. ADT is used in combination with local therapy in high-risk cases but is never sufficient as monotherapy in curative settings.

A 71-year-old man with metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer presents with worsening back pain. Imaging confirms progression of multiple osteoblastic bone metastases without visceral or nodal involvement. He has been on enzalutamide for 8 months with prior response, but now exhibits symptomatic skeletal progression. He has a history of severe osteonecrosis of the jaw following a dental extraction while on a bisphosphonate for osteoporosis; the lesion remains unhealed. His performance status is good, and he has no contraindications to radiopharmaceutical therapy. Radium-223 is considered appropriate for his symptomatic bone-predominant disease. Concurrently, a 68-year-old man with metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer on abiraterone acetate for 14 months undergoes routine imaging, which reveals two new asymptomatic bone metastases in the thoracic spine and ribs. His primary tumor and pelvic lymph nodes are stable, PSA has risen from 2.1 to 4.5 ng/mL, and he remains asymptomatic with excellent performance status. There is no visceral disease. The clinical team evaluates options for both patients, focusing on optimal integration of systemic therapy, bone-targeting agents, and local interventions.

**Select all that apply:**
A. Initiate radium-223 concurrently with enzalutamide and initiate mandatory denosumab.
B. Initiate radium-223 monotherapy and withhold denosumab due to elevated toxicity risk.
C. Perform metastasis-directed therapy to the progressing lesions and continue current systemic therapy.
D. Initiate radium-223 concurrently with abiraterone and initiate mandatory denosumab.
E. Withhold metastasis-directed therapy and transition to an alternative systemic therapy or clinical trial.
F. Initiate radium-223 concurrently with docetaxel and withhold denosumab.

**Answer:** A, C

**Rationale:**
Option A is correct because current evidence supports the cautious use of radium-223 in combination with enzalutamide, particularly in patients with symptomatic bone metastases. Unlike the combination with abiraterone, which is associated with increased fractures and mortality, concurrent use with enzalutamide does not carry the same level of risk when managed appropriately. Furthermore, guidelines now mandate the use of bone-modifying agents such as denosumab in all patients receiving radium-223 to reduce skeletal-related events, even in those with a history of osteonecrosis of the jaw, as the risk of pathological fracture outweighs the risk of ONJ progression. Option B is incorrect because withholding denosumab increases the risk of skeletal complications, including fractures, which counteracts the therapeutic benefit of radium-223. The current standard requires universal use of bone-protective agents during radium-223 therapy regardless of prior ONJ, making monotherapy without such agents unsafe.
