Option E is incorrect. Bevacizumab is an anti-angiogenic agent that is strictly contraindicated in patients with squamous cell carcinoma of the lung. Its use in squamous histology is associated with an unacceptably high risk of severe, life-threatening pulmonary hemorrhage (hemoptysis). Current medical practice restricts bevacizumab exclusively to non-squamous NSCLC.

Option F is incorrect. Pemetrexed is an antifolate chemotherapy agent whose efficacy is confined to non-squamous NSCLC (such as adenocarcinoma). It is not indicated, either as front-line or maintenance therapy, for patients with squamous cell carcinoma due to a well-documented lack of efficacy in this histologic subtype.

A 55-year-old male with a history of orthotopic heart transplantation presents with persistent fever, night sweats, and a progressively enlarging right cervical lymph node. He is 3 years post-transplant and has been on maintenance immunosuppression with tacrolimus and mycophenolate mofetil. Physical examination reveals a 4 cm firm, non-tender cervical lymph node. Laboratory studies show mild anemia and elevated LDH. PET/CT demonstrates hypermetabolic cervical, mediastinal, and axillary lymphadenopathy with no evidence of extranodal involvement. An excisional lymph node biopsy confirms monomorphic post-transplant lymphoproliferative disorder (PTLD) of diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL) type, with strong immunoreactivity for CD20 and in situ hybridization positive for Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) RNA. Reduction of immunosuppression is initiated. Given the aggressive histology, he receives induction therapy with four weekly doses of rituximab. Interim imaging after induction shows partial metabolic response but residual hypermetabolic lymphadenopathy. His echocardiogram demonstrates preserved left ventricular ejection fraction of 60%, and renal and hepatic functions are within normal limits. The multidisciplinary transplant oncology team discusses escalation to systemic chemoimmunotherapy. The patient is eligible for combination therapy and has no contraindications to cytotoxic agents. The team considers various regimens, including those recently evaluated in de novo DLBCL, while weighing the unique risks of allograft dysfunction and infection in the post-transplant setting. The goal is to select a regimen with proven efficacy in aggressive B-cell PTLD while minimizing toxicity to the cardiac allograft and other organs.

**Select all that apply:**
A. Initiate R-CHOP (rituximab, cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, vincristine, prednisone) as concurrent chemoimmunotherapy
B. Initiate polatuzumab vedotin in combination with R-CHP (rituximab, cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, prednisone)
C. Continue observation with further reduction of immunosuppression and close monitoring
D. Administer consolidation with rituximab monotherapy following induction
E. Proceed with anti-CD19 chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T-cell therapy with protocolized immunosuppression management
F. Refer for autologous hematopoietic cell transplantation

**Answer:** A

**Rationale:**
Option A is correct. R-CHOP remains the standard of care for systemic monomorphic PTLD of DLBCL subtype that fails to achieve complete response after initial reduction of immunosuppression and rituximab induction. The PTLD-1 trial and subsequent consensus guidelines support anthracycline-based chemoimmunotherapy as the cornerstone of treatment in high-risk patients. This regimen has demonstrated efficacy in achieving durable remissions while maintaining a manageable toxicity profile in solid organ transplant recipients when carefully monitored.

Option B is incorrect. Although polatuzumab vedotin plus R-CHP has shown improved progression-free survival in previously untreated de novo DLBCL in the POLARIX trial, this regimen has not been validated in the PTLD population. The underlying pathophysiology of PTLD differs significantly from de novo DLBCL, particularly in the context of chronic immunosuppression and EBV-driven lymphomagenesis. There are no clinical trials supporting the use of polatuzumab vedotin in PTLD, and its integration into standard practice for this population remains investigational.

Option C is incorrect. Continued observation is not appropriate in a patient with residual metabolic disease after induction therapy. Polymorphic PTLD in complete remission may be managed with observation and reduced immunosuppression, but this patient has monomorphic DLBCL-type PTLD with only a partial response. Active disease warrants escalation to cytotoxic therapy to prevent progression and improve survival outcomes.

Option D is incorrect. Consolidation with rituximab monotherapy is not indicated after incomplete response to initial rituximab induction in aggressive monomorphic PTLD. There is no evidence that additional anti-CD20 therapy alone can overcome resistance to prior rituximab in the setting of residual disease. This approach would delay effective cytotoxic therapy and increase the risk of disease progression.

Option E is incorrect. Anti-CD19 CAR T-cell therapy is currently recommended for relapsed or refractory PTLD after failure of frontline chemoimmunotherapy, not as initial systemic treatment. While it has shown promise in the salvage setting, its use upfront is not supported by evidence and poses unnecessary risks of cytokine release syndrome and neurotoxicity in a patient who is likely to respond to standard chemoimmunotherapy.

Option F is incorrect. Autologous hematopoietic cell transplantation is not recommended in solid organ transplant recipients due to high non-relapse mortality, primarily from infections and allograft loss. It is generally avoided in this population and has been supplanted by cellular therapies like CAR T cells in the relapsed setting. It has no role as initial therapy for PTLD.

A 63-year-old male with a 40-pack-year smoking history presents for follow-up after undergoing a right upper lobectomy with complete mediastinal lymph node dissection for a 4.2 cm squamous cell carcinoma of the lung. Final pathology reveals negative surgical margins and no lymph node metastases (pT2bN0M0, Stage IB). His pulmonary function tests are within acceptable limits, and he has recovered well from surgery with an Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group (ECOG) performance status of 0. He has no significant comorbidities and is eager to pursue any treatment that may improve his long-term survival. A multidisciplinary tumor board reviews his case, noting the tumor size exceeds 4 cm, and discusses the role of adjuvant therapy. Separately, a 58-year-old male with a 3 cm lung adenocarcinoma underwent a left lower lobectomy with complete resection (R0) and was found to have pT1cN1M0 disease involving a single hilar lymph node. He completed four cycles of adjuvant cisplatin and pemetrexed without complications and is now asymptomatic with an ECOG performance status of 0. The team considers whether additional therapy is warranted. Additionally, a 68-year-old female never-smoker presents with a 5.5 cm right lung mass, bilateral pulmonary nodules, and multiple hepatic lesions on CT imaging. A liver biopsy confirms metastatic lung adenocarcinoma. She reports worsening cough, dyspnea, and a 10-pound weight loss over the past two months. Her ECOG performance status is 1, and she has no prior cancer history. The oncology team initiates workup to determine the most appropriate initial management strategy.

**Select all that apply:**
A. Observation
B. Adjuvant platinum-based chemotherapy
C. Comprehensive biomarker testing to guide targeted therapy or immunotherapy
D. Postoperative radiotherapy (PORT)
E. First-line platinum-based chemotherapy with or without immunotherapy
F. Adjuvant platinum-based chemotherapy followed by postoperative radiotherapy (PORT)

**Answer:** B, A, C

**Rationale:**
The management of non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) requires precise integration of surgical pathology, disease stage, and molecular profiling to optimize outcomes while minimizing unnecessary toxicity. For the first patient with completely resected Stage IB (pT2bN0M0) squamous cell carcinoma measuring 4.2 cm, adjuvant platinum-based chemotherapy (Option B) is indicated. Modern evidence, including updated analyses of the JBR.10 trial, demonstrates a survival benefit with adjuvant chemotherapy in patients with Stage IB NSCLC who have high-risk features, particularly tumor size ≥4 cm. This represents a refinement from earlier interpretations that dismissed adjuvant chemotherapy for all Stage IB patients, as current guidelines support treatment intensification in this higher-risk subgroup. Observation (Option A) would be appropriate only for lower-risk Stage IB tumors (e.g., <4 cm), which does not apply here. Postoperative radiotherapy (Option D) is not recommended for pN0 disease, as it confers no survival benefit and increases toxicity, particularly in patients with negative margins. The combination of chemotherapy and PORT (Option F) is unsupported in this setting and amplifies risks without evidence of benefit. For the second patient with pT1cN1M0 adenocarcinoma who has already completed adjuvant chemotherapy, observation (Option A) is the correct next step. Current data, including the LungART trial, show no overall survival benefit from PORT in completely resected N1 disease and suggest increased pulmonary and cardiac toxicity. Historically, PORT was more commonly used in node-positive cases, but modern standards reserve it for select pN2 or margin-positive cases. Adjuvant chemotherapy (Option B) has already been completed, so repeating or continuing it is not indicated. Adding PORT (Option D or F) would expose the patient to unnecessary risks without proven benefit. For the third patient with metastatic lung adenocarcinoma, comprehensive biomarker testing (Option C) is essential before initiating systemic therapy. This includes testing for EGFR, ALK, ROS1, BRAF, MET, RET, NTRK, and PD-L1 expression, especially in never-smokers with non-squamous histology. Targeted therapies and immunotherapy have transformed outcomes in advanced NSCLC, and treatment selection must be biomarker-driven to maximize efficacy. Initiating first-line platinum-based chemotherapy with or without immunotherapy (Option E) without prior biomarker results risks delaying or precluding the use of more effective targeted agents. While chemotherapy may eventually be part of the regimen, it should not precede molecular profiling. Observation (Option A) is inappropriate in the setting of symptomatic metastatic disease requiring active treatment. Adjuvant chemotherapy (Option B) is not applicable in Stage IV disease, as it is defined for post-resection settings. Thus, the correct actions are adjuvant chemotherapy for the high-risk Stage IB patient, observation after completed adjuvant therapy in N1 disease, and biomarker testing in metastatic adenocarcinoma.

A 68-year-old man presents with a rising PSA five years after completing definitive external beam radiotherapy for localized prostate cancer. He is otherwise in stable health but has a history of severe metabolic syndrome, osteopenia, and a prior episode of clinical depression that was exacerbated during a brief trial of androgen deprivation therapy (ADT) years ago. A PSMA-PET scan demonstrates focal radiotracer uptake confined to the right lobe of the prostate, with no evidence of regional lymph node involvement or distant metastatic disease. A subsequent targeted biopsy confirms recurrent Gleason 4+3=7 adenocarcinoma. The multidisciplinary tumor board determines that he is a candidate for salvage high-dose-rate (HDR) brachytherapy. The radiation oncology team plans to deliver a curative-intent reirradiation course and seeks guidance on the optimal systemic treatment strategy during this period. The patient expresses concern about the side effects of hormone therapy but is highly motivated to maximize his chance of long-term disease control. Concurrently, a 72-year-old man with metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer (mCRPC) on long-term ADT and enzalutamide presents for follow-up after two years of stable disease. His PSA has recently shown a slight but measurable increase. Staging with CT chest, abdomen, and pelvis reveals two new 1.2 cm pulmonary nodules in the right lower lobe, while the bone scan shows no progression in previously identified sclerotic lesions in the axial skeleton. He remains asymptomatic and strongly wishes to avoid initiating cytotoxic chemotherapy. The radiation oncology team confirms that the lung lesions are technically amenable to stereotactic body radiotherapy (SBRT) with high precision and minimal risk to surrounding lung tissue.

**Select all that apply:**
A. Proceed with salvage prostate reirradiation with the concurrent addition of androgen deprivation therapy (ADT).
B. Proceed with salvage prostate reirradiation without the concurrent addition of androgen deprivation therapy (ADT).
C. Forgo metastasis-directed therapy (MDT) and immediately transition to a new line of systemic therapy.
D. Proceed with metastasis-directed therapy (MDT) to the isolated visceral lesions to delay transitioning systemic therapy.
E. Decline metastasis-directed therapy (MDT) as the patient exceeds the threshold of 5 metastatic lesions on conventional imaging.
F. Offer metastasis-directed therapy (MDT) based on favorable disease tempo despite exceeding 5 lesions on conventional imaging.

**Answer:** A, C

**Rationale:**
In the first patient, salvage reirradiation for localized prostate recurrence is a potentially curative option. Current evidence supports the integration of androgen deprivation therapy (ADT) during this phase, extrapolating from robust data in the definitive radiotherapy setting where ADT significantly improves biochemical and long-term oncologic outcomes. Although this patient has comorbidities and a history of mood disturbance linked to prior ADT, the modern standard emphasizes that the oncologic benefit of combining ADT with reirradiation likely outweighs the risks in most patients, particularly when long-term control is the goal. Therefore, adding ADT is considered a standard component of treatment. Withholding ADT, while historically considered in high-risk patients for toxicity, is no longer recommended as a routine approach due to the anticipated improvement in disease control.
Option B is incorrect because it reflects an older, more conservative strategy that individualized ADT use based on patient risk factors and toxicity concerns. While minimizing treatment burden is important, contemporary management prioritizes maximizing tumor control by routinely incorporating ADT during salvage reirradiation, even in patients with comorbidities, unless contraindicated.
Option C is correct for the second patient, who has oligoprogressive mCRPC with new visceral metastases in the lungs. The presence of visceral disease, even if limited in number and asymptomatic, is a well-established indicator of aggressive tumor biology and higher risk of systemic progression. Guidelines do not support the use of metastasis-directed therapy (MDT) in this context to delay systemic therapy escalation. Instead, the standard is to promptly transition to the next line of systemic treatment, such as chemotherapy or an alternative androgen receptor pathway inhibitor, to address the systemic nature of the disease.
Option D is incorrect because it suggests using MDT to delay systemic therapy in the presence of visceral metastases. While MDT can be effective for nodal or bone-only oligoprogression, its use in visceral sites like the lung is not supported by evidence for disease modification or survival benefit. Relying on local therapy in this setting may lead to undertreatment of systemic disease.
Option E is incorrect because the patient has only two metastatic lesions on conventional imaging, well below the typical threshold of five. Even if the count were higher, the decision to offer MDT would depend on disease tempo and site, but in this case, the limiting factor is visceral involvement, not lesion number.
Option F is incorrect because while disease tempo is favorable, the presence of visceral metastases overrides considerations of lesion burden or stability. Favorable kinetics do not negate the poor prognostic implications of visceral spread in prostate cancer, and MDT should not be used to defer systemic therapy in such cases.

A 59-year-old woman with metastatic uterine leiomyosarcoma has progressed after six cycles of doxorubicin-based chemotherapy. She is now seeking further systemic treatment. Tumor genomic profiling reveals a tumor mutational burden (TMB) of 14 mutations per megabase (mut/Mb), classifying the tumor as TMB-high (TMB-H). Mismatch repair proteins are intact (pMMR), and no other actionable alterations, including NTRK fusions or BRCA mutations, are detected. The patient expresses strong interest in immunotherapy and specifically inquires about combination checkpoint inhibition, having read that dual-agent regimens may enhance antitumor activity. She is otherwise in good performance status and has no significant autoimmune history. Concurrently, a 42-year-old premenopausal woman is diagnosed with unresectable, low-grade endometrial stromal sarcoma that is estrogen and progesterone receptor-positive. Due to extensive intra-abdominal adhesions from prior surgeries, bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy is considered too high-risk. The oncology team plans to initiate aromatase inhibitor therapy. Additionally, a 65-year-old woman undergoes simulation for adjuvant pelvic radiation therapy following complete resection of a high-grade uterine sarcoma. The radiation oncologist is delineating target volumes and notes significant daily variation in vaginal cuff position due to bladder and rectal filling. An additional volume must be defined to account for this physiological motion to ensure adequate coverage of tissues at risk for microscopic disease.

**Select all that apply:**
A. Initiate pembrolizumab monotherapy for the 59-year-old patient with TMB-H uterine leiomyosarcoma
B. Initiate ipilimumab plus nivolumab for the 59-year-old patient with TMB-H uterine leiomyosarcoma
C. Prescribe letrozole plus leuprolide acetate for the 42-year-old premenopausal patient with ER/PR-positive endometrial stromal sarcoma
D. Prescribe letrozole monotherapy for the 42-year-old premenopausal patient with ER/PR-positive endometrial stromal sarcoma
E. Define the internal target volume (ITV) as encompassing the full range of motion and consider it equivalent to the clinical target volume (CTV) for the 65-year-old patient undergoing adjuvant radiation
F. Define the internal target volume (ITV) as a separate expansion margin added to the clinical target volume (CTV) to account for organ motion in the 65-year-old patient

**Answer:** A, C, E

**Rationale:**
For the 59-year-old patient with TMB-H metastatic uterine leiomyosarcoma, pembrolizumab monotherapy is an FDA-approved, tumor-agnostic treatment for patients with unresectable or metastatic solid tumors harboring TMB-H (≥10 mut/Mb), regardless of tumor type. This approval is based on robust clinical evidence demonstrating durable responses in biomarker-selected populations, making it a guideline-endorsed standard of care. Although the patient expresses interest in combination immunotherapy, ipilimumab plus nivolumab lacks regulatory approval and clinical validation for TMB-H uterine sarcomas. While this combination is effective in other biomarker-defined contexts such as dMMR/MSI-H tumors, it is not recognized as a standard therapy for TMB-H in this histology, and its use would be off-label and unsupported by current evidence. For the 42-year-old premenopausal patient with hormone receptor-positive endometrial stromal sarcoma, concurrent use of an aromatase inhibitor and a GnRH agonist like leuprolide acetate is required to achieve ovarian suppression and prevent compensatory estrogen production. Aromatase inhibitors alone are ineffective in premenopausal women because ovarian steroidogenesis remains intact, leading to continued estrogen synthesis that counteracts the drug’s effect. Therefore, combining letrozole with leuprolide acetate provides effective endocrine suppression and aligns with current standards for premenopausal patients who are not candidates for surgical oophorectomy. In contrast, letrozole monotherapy would be inadequate due to persistent ovarian function and is not supported in this population. For the 65-year-old patient undergoing adjuvant pelvic radiation, the internal target volume (ITV) should account for interfraction anatomical variation, particularly in the position of the vaginal cuff due to variable bladder and rectal filling. Modern radiation oncology protocols for post-hysterectomy patients recognize that the ITV, which includes the full range of motion, should be treated as the clinical target volume (CTV) to ensure consistent coverage of microscopic disease. This approach acknowledges the limitations of rigid geometric expansions and prioritizes robust target coverage in the context of significant organ motion. Defining the ITV as a separate margin added to the CTV reflects an outdated, additive model based on older ICRU recommendations and does not align with current practice for uterine cancers, where functional equivalence between ITV and CTV is standard to mitigate the risk of geographic miss.

A 45-year-old male with no significant past medical history presents with rapid-onset abdominal distension and B symptoms over two weeks. Imaging reveals a 12 cm mesenteric mass with no evidence of bowel obstruction. Serum LDH is markedly elevated at 1,850 U/L (normal <250). A core needle biopsy confirms Burkitt lymphoma with characteristic 'starry sky' histology. Immunophenotyping shows CD20+, CD10+, BCL6+, BCL2–, and Ki-67 index >99%. FISH analysis detects a MYC::IGH rearrangement. Staging lumbar puncture shows no cytologic or flow cytometric evidence of CNS involvement. His ECOG performance status is 0, and organ function is normal. The oncology team initiates treatment planning and discusses appropriate induction therapy and CNS-directed prophylaxis. A multidisciplinary meeting considers whether intrathecal chemotherapy should be included and whether systemic high-dose methotrexate is necessary. Separately, a 28-year-old male presents with right jaw swelling and rapidly progressive cervical lymphadenopathy. Excisional biopsy demonstrates Burkitt lymphoma with identical immunophenotypic and molecular features. The pathology team considers whether EBER-ISH testing is required before finalizing the diagnosis. Concurrently, a 35-year-old female underwent complete surgical resection of a 4 cm localized ovarian mass, confirmed as Burkitt lymphoma. Postoperative staging shows no residual disease, normal LDH, and negative CSF flow cytometry. She is classified as low-risk and scheduled to begin DA-EPOCH-R. The team debates the necessity and components of CNS prophylaxis in her case, particularly given the absence of high-risk features.

**Select all that apply:**
A. Initiate DA-EPOCH-R without intrathecal prophylaxis in the 35-year-old female with low-risk, resected disease.
B. Defer EBER-ISH testing in the 28-year-old male, as it does not alter initial treatment decisions.
C. Administer high-dose systemic methotrexate and intrathecal methotrexate or cytarabine as part of CNS prophylaxis for all patients, including those on DA-EPOCH-R.
D. Use DA-EPOCH-R because it is specifically designed for patients who cannot tolerate more intensive regimens like CODOX-M/IVAC or R-hyperCVAD.
E. Proceed with intrathecal chemotherapy in the 45-year-old male despite negative CSF, given the high-risk nature of his disease.
F. Omit high-dose systemic methotrexate in DA-EPOCH-R–based therapy, as this regimen does not require it for effective CNS prophylaxis.

**Answer:** B, C, E

**Rationale:**
Option A is incorrect. Although the 35-year-old female has low-risk, resected disease, current standards emphasize that all patients with Burkitt lymphoma require adequate CNS prophylaxis regardless of risk stratification. Omitting intrathecal therapy, even in low-risk cases, increases the risk of CNS relapse due to the aggressive biology of the disease. The approach of withholding prophylaxis based on risk is outdated and no longer supported by contemporary protocols. Option B is correct. EBER-ISH testing identifies EBV association, which can subclassify Burkitt lymphoma into endemic or sporadic forms, but it does not influence initial treatment selection. Modern chemoimmunotherapy regimens are equally effective regardless of EBV status, and delaying or modifying therapy based on EBER results is not indicated. Testing may be performed for epidemiologic or research purposes but is not mandatory for treatment initiation. Option C is correct. Robust CNS prophylaxis is now considered essential across all treatment regimens, including DA-EPOCH-R. This includes both high-dose systemic methotrexate and intrathecal chemotherapy (methotrexate and/or cytarabine), even when the systemic regimen does not inherently contain high-dose methotrexate. This standardized approach aims to prevent CNS relapse, which remains a critical determinant of long-term survival. Option D is correct in context but not a therapeutic action—however, it reflects appropriate patient selection for DA-EPOCH-R. While not a direct management step, it acknowledges that DA-EPOCH-R is often preferred in patients with comorbidities or lower tolerance for extreme intensity. Yet, even in this setting, CNS prophylaxis must still be fully implemented. Option E is correct. Despite negative CSF cytology, the 45-year-old male has multiple high-risk features—large tumor burden, elevated LDH, and B symptoms—making him at substantial risk for occult CNS involvement. Intrathecal chemotherapy is a cornerstone of prophylaxis and should not be omitted based on negative initial lumbar puncture. Option F is incorrect. While DA-EPOCH-R does not include high-dose methotrexate in its backbone, this does not eliminate the need for it in CNS prophylaxis. Relying solely on the regimen’s systemic penetration is insufficient. Current guidelines mandate the addition of high-dose systemic methotrexate and intrathecal therapy irrespective of the primary regimen to ensure adequate CNS protection.

A 58-year-old male presents 2 years after total gastrectomy for stage II gastric adenocarcinoma with chronic bloating, postprandial abdominal discomfort, and watery diarrhea occurring multiple times daily. He reports symptom exacerbation after carbohydrate-rich meals. Physical examination reveals mild epigastric tenderness without rebound or guarding. There is no weight loss, fever, or blood in the stool. Small intestinal bacterial overgrowth (SIBO) is clinically suspected. He has no known drug allergies and is not currently on any gastrointestinal medications. In addition, a 45-year-old premenopausal female, 14 months post-subtotal gastrectomy for gastric cancer, is on monthly intramuscular vitamin B12 injections and remains asymptomatic. She has no history of fractures, bone pain, or falls. She asks about appropriate long-term monitoring for nutritional and skeletal health. Separately, a 62-year-old female, 3 years post-gastrectomy, completed adjuvant oxaliplatin-based chemotherapy 28 months ago. She reports persistent numbness and tingling in her fingertips, which interfere with fine motor tasks such as buttoning clothes and typing. She explicitly denies any burning, aching, or lancinating pain in her extremities. Neurological examination confirms distal symmetric sensory loss in a stocking-glove distribution, with preserved strength and normal deep tendon reflexes.

**Select all that apply:**
A. Initiate empiric rifaximin 550 mg TID for 7–10 days and advise a generic high-protein, low-carbohydrate diet
B. Perform breath testing to guide a 14-day antibiotic course and recommend a low-FODMAP diet
C. Schedule bone density testing at 3 years post-gastrectomy and omit routine B12 monitoring while on parenteral therapy
D. Obtain a DEXA scan now and monitor serum vitamin B12 levels annually despite parenteral therapy
E. Withhold duloxetine, as it is indicated strictly for painful neuropathy and is ineffective for numbness
F. Initiate a trial of duloxetine to potentially improve functional impairment and overall quality of life

**Answer:** A, C, E

**Rationale:**
The management of long-term complications following gastrectomy requires a nuanced, evidence-based approach across gastrointestinal, nutritional, and neurologic domains. For the patient with suspected small intestinal bacterial overgrowth (SIBO), empiric treatment with rifaximin 550 mg three times daily for 7 to 10 days is currently recommended as first-line therapy. This approach avoids delays associated with breath testing, which has variable sensitivity and specificity and does not consistently alter outcomes when used to guide therapy. Concomitant dietary counseling to reduce fermentable substrates through a high-protein, low-carbohydrate diet helps minimize symptom recurrence. Therefore, Option A aligns with current standards and is appropriate.

Option B recommends breath testing followed by a 14-day antibiotic course and a low-FODMAP diet. While historically used, this approach is no longer favored due to the diagnostic limitations of breath testing and the lack of evidence that targeted therapy improves long-term outcomes over empiric treatment. The additional burden of dietary restriction and testing delays make this an outdated strategy, particularly in patients with classic post-gastrectomy symptoms.

For the asymptomatic premenopausal woman on parenteral vitamin B12, bone health surveillance should be timed strategically. Current guidelines recommend scheduling the first DEXA scan at 3 years post-gastrectomy in asymptomatic patients, as bone loss typically progresses gradually. Earlier scanning does not improve outcomes and increases unnecessary testing. Furthermore, routine monitoring of serum B12 levels is not indicated in patients receiving regular parenteral replacement, as levels do not correlate reliably with tissue stores or clinical status, and the treatment regimen is already established. Thus, Option C is correct.

Option D advocates for immediate DEXA scanning and annual B12 monitoring despite parenteral therapy. This reflects an older paradigm that emphasized frequent surveillance without evidence of clinical benefit. Immediate bone density assessment is not cost-effective in low-risk, asymptomatic individuals, and annual phlebotomy for B12 levels adds burden without guiding management when replacement is already optimized.

Option G is not listed in the final options, but Option D and similar approaches represent over-monitoring. Regarding neuropathy, the patient describes pure sensory dysfunction with numbness and functional impairment but no pain. Duloxetine is the only pharmacologic agent with proven efficacy in chemotherapy-induced peripheral neuropathy, but its benefit is limited to painful symptoms. Multiple randomized trials have shown no improvement in numbness, paresthesia, or motor function with duloxetine, and its use in non-painful neuropathy exposes patients to unnecessary side effects such as nausea, fatigue, and increased fall risk. Therefore, withholding duloxetine is the appropriate course, making Option E correct.

Option F suggests initiating duloxetine to improve quality of life despite the absence of pain. While neuropathy impacts function, current evidence does not support off-label use of duloxetine for non-painful symptoms. Prior studies evaluating its use in pure sensory neuropathy failed to demonstrate meaningful benefit, and guidelines strictly reserve its use for painful neuropathic conditions. Initiating therapy in this context would constitute inappropriate polypharmacy.

A 64-year-old man with chronic hepatitis C virus and Child-Pugh A cirrhosis presents to the clinic for restaging. He was initially diagnosed with stage IVB hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) with pulmonary metastases and was treated with first-line atezolizumab plus bevacizumab. He reports mild fatigue but maintains an excellent performance status. Recent computed tomography (CT) imaging demonstrates significant enlargement of the hepatic lesions and new pulmonary nodules, consistent with disease progression. Laboratory evaluation reveals a total bilirubin of 1.0 mg/dL and an alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) level of 250 ng/mL. The multidisciplinary tumor board is discussing the next steps in management, specifically regarding the utility of tumor molecular profiling and subsequent systemic therapy selection. Which of the following statements represent appropriate management steps for this patient?

**Select all that apply:**
A. Submit the tumor tissue for microsatellite instability (MSI) or mismatch repair (MMR) testing to identify eligibility for targeted immune checkpoint inhibitors.
B. Decline MSI and MMR testing, as there is no established clinical indication or role for this specific biomarker testing in hepatocellular carcinoma.
C. Consider administration of dostarlimab-gxly if the patient's tumor demonstrates an MSI-H or dMMR phenotype.
D. Initiate cabozantinib as subsequent-line therapy without pursuing MSI/MMR testing, given the lack of established routine molecular profiling.
E. Perform routine testing for programmed death ligand 1 (PD-L1) expression to determine eligibility for single-agent pembrolizumab.
F. Administer ramucirumab as subsequent-line therapy since it is indicated for all patients progressing on first-line immunotherapy regardless of biomarker status.

**Answer:** B, C, D

**Rationale:**
The management of advanced hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) following progression on first-line systemic therapy, such as atezolizumab plus bevacizumab, requires the selection of subsequent-line agents based on liver function, performance status, and specific clinical parameters. For a patient with preserved Child-Pugh A liver function and disease progression, several active subsequent-line therapies are available, including tyrosine kinase inhibitors like cabozantinib. A unique and often misunderstood aspect of HCC management involves the role of molecular biomarkers. In many solid tumors, routine profiling for microsatellite instability (MSI) or mismatch repair (MMR) represents standard practice to identify candidates for immune checkpoint inhibition. However, current medical consensus clearly establishes that routine testing for MSI, MMR, tumor mutational burden (TMB), or programmed death ligand 1 (PD-L1) has no established role in HCC, as immunotherapies have demonstrated broad efficacy regardless of these biomarker statuses. Nevertheless, a clinical nuance exists: if a tumor is incidentally known to possess an MSI-H/dMMR phenotype, specific therapies tailored to that profile, such as dostarlimab-gxly, remain appropriate options. Therefore, the optimal approach involves proceeding with standard subsequent-line therapies without mandating routine molecular profiling, while correctly applying biomarker-specific treatments only if such genomic data is already available.

Option B is correct. Aligning with contemporary clinical evidence, there is no established role for routine MSI, MMR, tumor mutational burden (TMB), or PD-L1 testing in the management of HCC. Treatment decisions should not be contingent upon these biomarker results, making it appropriate to decline routine testing.

Option C is correct. This highlights a nuanced clinical reality: despite the lack of an indication for routine testing, if a patient's tumor is incidentally known to harbor an MSI-H or dMMR phenotype (for example, via broad genomic profiling obtained for atypical presentations or clinical trials), dostarlimab-gxly remains a valid and recommended subsequent-line therapy for such molecularly defined tumors.

Option D is correct. Cabozantinib is a preferred subsequent-line therapy with proven survival benefits for patients who have progressed on prior systemic regimens. Initiating this effective targeted therapy without delaying care for unestablished routine molecular profiling is the optimal, evidence-based management strategy.

Option A is incorrect. Historically, or when extrapolating from pan-tumor oncology principles, one might assume that MSI or MMR testing is a mandatory clinical indication in advanced HCC to select candidates for immunotherapy. However, current evidence has evolved to show that immune checkpoint inhibitors provide robust clinical benefit in HCC without the need for MSI, MMR, or PD-L1 selection. Consequently, routine testing for these biomarkers is not established or recommended.

Option E is incorrect. Unlike certain other malignancies where PD-L1 expression is a prerequisite for immunotherapy, PD-L1 testing has no established clinical utility in HCC. Immune checkpoint inhibitors are effective and indicated independently of PD-L1 expression levels.

Option F is incorrect. Ramucirumab is an effective subsequent-line option, but its clinical benefit is exclusively demonstrated in patients with a baseline alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) level of ≥400 ng/mL. Because this patient presents with an AFP of 250 ng/mL, ramucirumab is clinically inappropriate.

A 68-year-old man with newly diagnosed blastic plasmacytoid dendritic cell neoplasm (BPDCN) completed initial induction therapy with tagraxofusp-erzs. He had multiple violaceous cutaneous plaques at presentation, including a prominent lesion on his back. Post-induction evaluation shows no morphologic evidence of disease in the bone marrow, and his peripheral blood counts have normalized, indicating hematologic remission. However, a protocol-mandated skin biopsy of the residual back lesion reveals persistent microscopic disease despite clinical improvement. The patient is otherwise asymptomatic, with preserved organ function and no signs of systemic progression. He remains eligible for further therapy and has tolerated tagraxofusp-erzs well without significant toxicity. The oncology team must determine the optimal next steps in management, considering whether to continue the current regimen, transition to alternative therapy, or proceed with consolidation. Given the unique biology of BPDCN and its propensity for extramedullary involvement, careful assessment of response criteria and timing of transplantation is critical. The team also considers long-term surveillance strategies in the context of prior cutaneous disease, weighing the utility of imaging versus clinical monitoring. Additionally, in a separate but related context, a 65-year-old woman with BPDCN and severe cytopenias is being evaluated for intensive chemotherapy due to unavailability of tagraxofusp-erzs. She has diffuse bruise-like skin lesions and is otherwise fit, with normal organ function. Her oncologist seeks the most effective induction regimen to achieve durable remission. Meanwhile, a 63-year-old woman, six months post-allogeneic hematopoietic cell transplantation (HCT) after achieving complete remission, is establishing a surveillance plan. She had isolated cutaneous lesions at diagnosis and remains in remission. Her team must decide on the optimal method for detecting early recurrence, particularly in extramedullary sites. These interconnected clinical decisions highlight the evolving standards in BPDCN management, particularly regarding response assessment, consolidation, and monitoring.

**Select all that apply:**
A. Continue current induction therapy with tagraxofusp-erzs for at least 4 additional cycles
B. Reclassify the disease as relapsed/refractory and initiate salvage therapy
C. Proceed with allogeneic hematopoietic cell transplantation in first remission
D. Proceed with autologous hematopoietic cell transplantation as consolidation
E. Use HyperCVAD as the preferred intensive chemotherapy regimen in patients not receiving tagraxofusp-erzs
F. Rely primarily on clinical skin examinations and targeted biopsies for post-remission surveillance

**Answer:** A, C, E

**Rationale:**
Continuing tagraxofusp-erzs for at least 4 additional cycles is appropriate when microscopic skin disease persists after initial therapy, despite hematologic remission. Skin clearance may lag behind marrow response, and extending the same regimen can lead to eventual complete clinical remission. Prematurely discontinuing an effective agent based on residual microscopic cutaneous findings may deny the patient a chance at deeper response. This approach is supported by recent clinical observations that distinguish transient residual skin involvement from true refractory disease.

Reclassifying the disease as relapsed or refractory at this stage is premature. While complete remission in BPDCN traditionally required full resolution of extramedullary disease, current practice recognizes that isolated microscopic skin persistence after otherwise effective induction does not necessarily indicate treatment failure. Switching to salvage therapy in this context would be inappropriate and could expose the patient to more toxic regimens unnecessarily, especially when the current therapy is well-tolerated and has induced hematologic remission.

Allogeneic hematopoietic cell transplantation remains the standard consolidation for eligible patients in first remission due to its potent graft-versus-leukemia effect, which reduces relapse risk. Given the aggressive nature of BPDCN and high relapse rates with chemotherapy alone, proceeding to allogeneic HCT offers the best chance for long-term disease control, even in patients with prior skin involvement.

Autologous hematopoietic cell transplantation lacks a graft-versus-leukemia effect and is associated with higher relapse rates in BPDCN. While it may be considered in patients who refuse or are ineligible for allogeneic HCT, it is not the preferred consolidation strategy for fit patients. Therefore, recommending autologous HCT over allogeneic HCT in a transplant-eligible patient is suboptimal.

HyperCVAD is a preferred intensive chemotherapy regimen for BPDCN in the absence of tagraxofusp-erzs. It has demonstrated superior response depth and durability compared to lymphoma-type regimens like CHOP. Given the patient’s fitness and preserved organ function, an ALL-type intensive protocol such as HyperCVAD offers the best chance for remission induction and bridging to transplantation.

Relying solely on clinical examination and biopsies for surveillance is insufficient for detecting early recurrence, particularly in patients with prior extramedullary disease. Routine whole-body FDG-PET/CT scans provide a more sensitive and standardized method for identifying occult cutaneous or systemic relapse, including in areas not clinically apparent. Therefore, physical exam and biopsy alone are inadequate as the primary surveillance strategy.

A 61-year-old female presents to the hematology/oncology clinic for a post-induction follow-up. Her medical history is notable for early-stage breast cancer treated 5 years ago with surgical resection followed by adjuvant doxorubicin, cyclophosphamide, and radiotherapy. One month ago, she presented with mucosal bleeding and fatigue. A bone marrow biopsy revealed 55% myeloblasts. Cytogenetic evaluation demonstrated inv(16)(p13.1q22), confirming a diagnosis of core binding factor (CBF) acute myeloid leukemia (AML). She completed standard intensive induction therapy with cytarabine and daunorubicin (7+3), and a repeat marrow confirms she has achieved a complete remission (CR). During counseling regarding consolidation therapy and her longitudinal management plan, she expresses concern about having a 'therapy-related' leukemia and asks how this diagnosis impacts her overall prognosis and how her treatment standards are maintained over time. Which of the following statements are appropriate to include in her counseling?

**Select all that apply:**
A. Inform her that despite her favorable cytogenetics, her long-term prognosis remains significantly inferior to that of patients with de novo CBF-AML due to her prior exposure to cytotoxic chemotherapy.
B. Inform her that her long-term prognosis is comparable to that of patients with de novo CBF-AML, provided she proceeds with optimal high-dose cytarabine-based consolidation.
C. Advise her that the evidence-based consensus guidelines governing her post-remission management are updated dynamically multiple times per year to rapidly integrate novel practice-changing trial data.
D. Advise her that the evidence-based consensus guidelines governing her post-remission management are reviewed and updated by an expert panel strictly on an annual schedule.
E. Explain that because her leukemia is therapy-related secondary to topoisomerase inhibitor and alkylator exposure, she must proceed directly to allogeneic hematopoietic cell transplantation in her first complete remission.
F. Reassure her that therapy-related leukemias associated with alkylating agents typically harbor favorable cytogenetic profiles and generally avoid the progressive, resistant disease course seen in de novo AML.

**Answer:** A, D

**Rationale:**
The overall management and counseling of a patient with therapy-related acute myeloid leukemia (t-AML) require a nuanced understanding of prognostic factors and guideline-driven care. Therapy-related AML arises as a complication of prior cytotoxic therapy, such as the alkylating agents and topoisomerase inhibitors commonly used in breast cancer treatment. While patients with core binding factor (CBF) AML—characterized by structural abnormalities like inv(16)—typically enjoy a favorable prognosis, the therapy-related nature of the disease introduces a more challenging clinical course. Current oncologic consensus maintains that even among patients with CBF translocations, those with therapy-related CBF-AML tend to have inferior outcomes compared to their counterparts with de novo disease. Consequently, accurate patient counseling must reflect this tempered prognosis. Furthermore, the standardization of care for such patients relies on authoritative consensus guidelines. To systematically review and integrate new clinical trial data and biologic insights, expert panels convene on a strictly annual schedule to update these diagnostic and therapeutic recommendations.

Option A is correct because current evidence confirms that therapy-related CBF-AML carries a less favorable prognosis than de novo CBF-AML. Despite the presence of favorable cytogenetics like inv(16), the background of prior cytotoxic exposure contributes to a disease biology that inherently reduces the likelihood of long-term survival compared to de novo cases.

Option B is incorrect. It reflects an outdated perspective positing that optimal intensive therapies, such as high-dose cytarabine consolidation, could completely abrogate the adverse prognostic impact of a therapy-related etiology in CBF-AML. Current medical understanding has evolved to recognize that while these patients still receive intensive consolidation, their clinical outcomes do not reach parity with those of de novo CBF-AML patients.

Option C is incorrect because it mischaracterizes the guideline update process. Although medical literature evolves continuously, the expert consensus panels responsible for these comprehensive AML guidelines do not update them dynamically multiple times throughout the year; rather, they adhere to a structured, annual review schedule.

Option D is correct as it accurately describes the formal review process for AML clinical practice guidelines. The expert panel convenes annually to evaluate recently published clinical trials and novel biologic factors, ensuring a rigorous, methodical update to the standard of care.

Option E is incorrect. While therapy-related AML generally has a poor prognosis, the presence of CBF translocations still places the patient in a relatively favorable risk category compared to other therapy-related leukemias. Consequently, proceeding directly to allogeneic hematopoietic cell transplantation in first complete remission is not universally mandated for CBF-AML; standard high-dose cytarabine-based consolidation remains an appropriate primary therapeutic strategy.

Option F is incorrect. Therapy-related leukemias associated with alkylating agents and topoisomerase inhibitors typically harbor unfavorable cytogenetic profiles, rather than favorable ones. Additionally, their disease course is characteristically progressive and more resistant to conventional cytotoxic therapies compared to de novo AML.

A 64-year-old man undergoes endoscopic mucosal resection for a 1.5 cm superficial esophageal lesion. Histopathology reveals well-differentiated squamous cell carcinoma with negative lateral and deep margins and no lymphovascular invasion. The depth of submucosal invasion is measured at 350 µm. A multidisciplinary tumor board reviews the case to determine further management. In a separate case, a 58-year-old woman is diagnosed with cT3N0 esophagogastric junction (EGJ) adenocarcinoma. Biopsy confirms diffuse-type histology with no distant metastases on staging. She has an excellent performance status and is medically fit for surgery. The oncology team discusses optimal perioperative therapy. Molecular profiling has not yet been performed. The tumor board considers whether immunotherapy should be added to perioperative chemotherapy and whether comprehensive genomic testing is warranted given the histology. Both cases prompt discussion about histology-specific thresholds for curative intent and appropriate integration of systemic therapies based on tumor biology.

**Select all that apply:**
A. Salvage esophagectomy or adjuvant chemoradiation
B. Routine endoscopic surveillance as adequately treated
C. Perioperative FLOT alone
D. Perioperative FLOT plus durvalumab
E. Upfront comprehensive Next-Generation Sequencing (NGS)
F. First-line therapy with pembrolizumab plus systemic chemotherapy

**Answer:** A, C, E

**Rationale:**
In the first case, the patient has a well-differentiated esophageal squamous cell carcinoma with submucosal invasion of 350 µm and no lymphovascular invasion. Although the margins are negative and the tumor is well-differentiated, the depth of invasion exceeds the critical threshold for low-risk disease in squamous histology. Unlike adenocarcinoma, where invasion <500 µm may be considered low-risk in the absence of adverse features, squamous cell carcinoma carries a significantly higher risk of nodal metastasis at depths ≥200 µm. Therefore, even with favorable differentiation and no LVI, invasion beyond 200 µm is classified as high-risk, warranting additional intervention such as salvage esophagectomy or adjuvant chemoradiation to address potential occult nodal disease. This approach is supported by current guidelines emphasizing histology-specific risk stratification.

Option B, routine endoscopic surveillance, would be appropriate only if the lesion were truly low-risk, which requires submucosal invasion <200 µm in squamous cell carcinoma. At 350 µm, this threshold is clearly exceeded, making surveillance alone inadequate and associated with unacceptably high recurrence rates. Choosing surveillance reflects an outdated application of adenocarcinoma-based criteria to squamous histology, which underestimates metastatic potential and compromises curative outcomes.

For the second patient with cT3N0 diffuse-type EGJ adenocarcinoma, perioperative chemotherapy with FLOT (5-FU, leucovorin, oxaliplatin, docetaxel) remains the standard of care. While immunotherapy has been integrated into perioperative regimens for certain subsets of gastric and EGJ cancers, recent phase III trials have not demonstrated a survival benefit with the addition of durvalumab to FLOT in patients with diffuse-type histology. The biological behavior of diffuse-type tumors may limit immune cell infiltration and response to checkpoint inhibitors, explaining the lack of efficacy. Therefore, adding durvalumab is not supported by current evidence and exposes the patient to unnecessary immune-related toxicities without proven benefit.

Option D, perioperative FLOT plus durvalumab, is an attractive choice given the success of immunotherapy in other gastrointestinal malignancies, but its indication is histology-dependent. In tumors with microsatellite instability or PD-L1 positivity, immunotherapy may play a role, but in diffuse-type adenocarcinoma without these features, the data do not justify routine use. This option represents an overextension of positive trial results to a population not shown to benefit.

Option F, first-line therapy with pembrolizumab plus chemotherapy, is approved in advanced gastric/GEJ adenocarcinoma with PD-L1 CPS ≥1 or MSI-H status. However, this patient has localized disease planned for surgical resection, and there is no indication for first-line systemic therapy outside the perioperative setting. Moreover, diffuse-type tumors are less likely to express PD-L1 or exhibit MSI-H, making this regimen unlikely to be effective. Administering it in place of perioperative FLOT would deviate from established curative-intent protocols.

Option E, upfront comprehensive NGS, is appropriate given the diagnostic uncertainty and potential therapeutic implications of molecular profiling. Diffuse-type gastric cancers may harbor CLDN18.2, HER2, or other targetable alterations, and identifying these can guide future therapy if recurrence occurs. Additionally, NGS can detect MSI-H or TMB-H status, which may influence adjuvant or palliative treatment decisions. While single-gene testing is still used in some centers, comprehensive profiling is increasingly recommended to avoid sequential delays and ensure all actionable targets are identified early, particularly in younger patients with aggressive histology.

A 68-year-old male presents with new-onset dysphagia and a 10-lb unintentional weight loss over two months. Upper endoscopy reveals a 1.8 cm irregular mucosal lesion in the distal esophagus. Biopsies confirm well-differentiated adenocarcinoma. Endoscopic ultrasound (EUS) shows tumor invasion into the submucosa without penetration of the muscularis propria (cT1b), and no suspicious lymph nodes (N0). He has not undergone cross-sectional imaging. The multidisciplinary team is evaluating staging. Separately, a 72-year-old female presents with progressive solid food dysphagia and regurgitation. Endoscopy identifies a large ulcerated mass in the middle esophagus; biopsy confirms squamous cell carcinoma. The lesion appears deeply invasive, and there is clinical concern for direct involvement of adjacent mediastinal structures such as the pericardium or trachea. Imaging to assess local invasion is needed. Additionally, a 55-year-old male with long-standing GERD undergoes surveillance endoscopy, revealing a 1.5 cm superficial nodular lesion within Barrett’s esophagus. Biopsy confirms adenocarcinoma. EUS indicates the lesion is confined to the mucosa (cT1a). The team must determine the most appropriate next steps for accurate staging and management across these cases, considering locoregional extent, depth of invasion, nodal involvement, and distant metastases. The goal is to guide treatment decisions with curative intent while avoiding unnecessary procedures.

**Select all that apply:**
A. Perform radiofrequency ablation (RFA) alone for the entire involved segment in the Barrett’s esophagus patient.
B. Perform endoscopic resection (ER) universally as it is an essential and mandatory staging requirement for all early-stage tumors (≤2 cm).
C. Rely on endoscopic ultrasound (EUS) for non-invasive T staging, utilizing ER primarily for therapeutic intent or to resolve specific diagnostic uncertainties.
D. Utilize FDG-PET/CT to definitively determine local invasion of the mediastinum in the patient with the bulky mid-esophageal tumor.
E. Utilize endoscopic ultrasound (EUS) and contrast-enhanced CT as the standard modalities to evaluate local mediastinal invasion.
F. Perform FDG-PET/CT as a routine component of the initial staging evaluation to rule out occult distant metastases in the cT1b adenocarcinoma patient.

**Answer:** C, E, F

**Rationale:**
Option A is incorrect because radiofrequency ablation (RFA) is contraindicated as first-line therapy in the presence of visible nodular lesions within Barrett’s esophagus. Such lesions carry a significant risk of harboring invasive carcinoma, and ablative therapy without prior histologic assessment via endoscopic resection (ER) may mask or undertreat submucosal disease. Current standards require ER for tissue acquisition to rule out deep invasion before any ablation is considered. Option B is incorrect because it promotes a universal, mandatory role for ER solely based on tumor size and clinical stage, which is no longer supported. While ER provides definitive histopathologic staging, it is not indicated indiscriminately for all cT1a or small cT1b lesions without prior non-invasive assessment. EUS remains the primary tool for initial T staging, and ER is reserved for cases where tissue confirmation is needed or when curative resection is feasible. Option C is correct because EUS is the modality of choice for initial non-invasive assessment of tumor depth in early esophageal cancers. ER should be used selectively—either to obtain accurate histology in cases of diagnostic uncertainty (e.g., distinguishing HGD from intramucosal cancer) or as definitive therapy for confirmed cT1a lesions. This approach avoids unnecessary invasive procedures while ensuring precise staging. Option D is incorrect because FDG-PET/CT lacks the spatial resolution to reliably differentiate direct tumor invasion of mediastinal structures from adjacent inflammatory or reactive changes. Although it shows high metabolic activity in tumors, it cannot anatomically delineate tumor margins from the pericardium, aorta, or airway. Relying on PET/CT for T4 staging may lead to inaccurate surgical planning or inappropriate exclusion from resection. Option E is correct because the combination of EUS and contrast-enhanced CT provides complementary data for assessing local tumor extent. EUS offers high-resolution imaging of the esophageal wall layers and regional lymph nodes, while CT demonstrates gross anatomical relationships and potential invasion into adjacent mediastinal structures. Together, they form the standard for evaluating suspected cT4 disease and guide decisions about resectability. Option F is correct because FDG-PET/CT is a standard component of initial staging for all patients with clinically invasive esophageal cancer (excluding purely superficial, incidentally found cT1a lesions). It detects occult distant metastases in a significant proportion of patients, particularly those with cT1b or higher disease, thereby preventing unnecessary curative-intent surgeries. Current guidelines recommend its routine use early in the staging pathway, rather than reserving it based on CT findings.

A 52-year-old female with a 5-year history of stage III follicular lymphoma presents with fevers, drenching night sweats, and a rapidly growing right cervical mass. Biopsy of the mass reveals high-grade B-cell lymphoma (HGBL). Fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) analysis is positive for rearrangements in MYC and BCL6, but negative for BCL2. She requires initial systemic therapy for the transformed disease. Twelve months later, she experiences a biopsy-proven chemosensitive relapse after initial therapy and is being evaluated for consolidative management.

**Select all that apply:**
A. For initial therapy, manage with an aggressive intensive chemoimmunotherapy regimen (e.g., DA-EPOCH-R), as HGBL with MYC and BCL6 rearrangements dictates the standard for aggressive treatment, similarly to true MYC and BCL2 double-hit lymphomas.
B. For initial therapy, administer standard anthracycline-based chemoimmunotherapy (e.g., R-CHOP), because HGBL with MYC and BCL6 rearrangements carries a more favorable prognosis and is managed similarly to DLBCL, NOS.
C. For consolidative therapy following her chemosensitive relapse, proceed with high-dose therapy and autologous stem cell rescue (HDT/ASCR), as it is a well-established, guideline-recommended standard of care in this setting.
D. For consolidative therapy following her chemosensitive relapse, avoid HDT/ASCR, as its efficacy in transformed follicular lymphoma lacks confirmation in prospective controlled studies, rendering its routine use investigational.
E. For initial therapy, administer single-agent lenalidomide, as HGBL with MYC and BCL6 rearrangements is indolent and does not require anthracycline-based regimens.
F. For consolidative therapy, proceed directly to active surveillance, as consolidative cellular therapies or transplants are strictly contraindicated following any chemosensitive relapse in HGBL.

**Answer:** B, C

**Rationale:**
The management of transformed follicular lymphoma (TFL) to high-grade B-cell lymphoma (HGBL) relies on precise molecular and histologic characterization. Historically, any lymphoma harboring concurrent MYC and BCL2 or BCL6 rearrangements was loosely grouped into a high-risk "double-hit" category, prompting the use of highly aggressive chemoimmunotherapy regimens like DA-EPOCH-R. However, our medical understanding has evolved. Recent updates in lymphoma classification clearly distinguish HGBL with isolated MYC and BCL6 rearrangements from true "double-hit" lymphomas (which harbor MYC and BCL2 rearrangements). Contemporary data confirm that MYC/BCL6-rearranged HGBL carries a more favorable prognosis that closely mirrors diffuse large B-cell lymphoma, not otherwise specified (DLBCL, NOS). Consequently, standard anthracycline-based chemoimmunotherapy such as R-CHOP is now recognized as the optimal initial treatment. Furthermore, in the event of a chemosensitive relapse, high-dose therapy with autologous stem cell rescue (HDT/ASCR) serves as a well-established, universally accepted standard of care for eligible patients. While skeptics previously cast doubt on this approach due to a lack of large-scale prospective randomized controlled trials specifically dedicated to transformed histologies, clinical practice firmly relies on robust retrospective data and extrapolation from de novo DLBCL paradigms to validate its efficacy.

Option A is incorrect because it reflects the outdated clinical practice of treating all dual-rearranged lymphomas with intensified regimens. We now understand that MYC/BCL6 rearrangements alone do not portend the same aggressive clinical course as MYC/BCL2 true double-hit lymphomas.

Option B aligns with current best practice. By recognizing the specific genetic profile of this patient's HGBL, standard anthracycline-based chemoimmunotherapy like R-CHOP is the appropriate initial therapy, sparing the patient unnecessary toxicity from intensified regimens.

Option C is correct as HDT/ASCR remains the cornerstone of consolidative therapy for patients with chemosensitive relapsed TFL. This approach offers a critical opportunity for durable remission and is strongly endorsed by clinical guidelines.

Option D is incorrect. Avoiding HDT/ASCR based solely on the absence of prospective controlled trials in transformed histologies represents a fundamental misunderstanding of clinical oncology standards. The procedure's clinical validity in this setting is firmly established through extensive retrospective cohorts and its proven success in aggressive B-cell lymphomas.

Option E is incorrect because newly transformed, rapidly growing HGBL mandates systemic combination chemoimmunotherapy. Single-agent immunomodulators like lenalidomide are reserved for select indolent or relapsed/refractory scenarios, not as initial therapy for an aggressive transformation.

Option F is incorrect because proceeding to active surveillance after a chemosensitive relapse in an aggressive lymphoma virtually guarantees a subsequent, likely refractory, relapse. Cellular therapies and auto-transplantation are highly indicated consolidation strategies in this exact scenario.

A 55-year-old male undergoes an endoscopic mucosal resection for a 2.5-cm sessile polyp in the descending colon. Pathologic examination reveals a well-differentiated adenocarcinoma invading through the muscularis mucosa into the submucosa (pT1). The distance from the deepest invasive tumor cells to the cauterized transection margin is 0.8 mm. There is no angiolymphatic invasion. Microscopic review at the advancing edge reveals ambiguous small clusters of cells (≤4 cells) suggestive of tumor budding. Which of the following pathologic interpretations and subsequent management steps are correct?

**Select all that apply:**
A. Classify the resection as having a positive margin, as the tumor cells are within 1 mm of the transected margin.
B. Classify the resection as having a negative margin, as the invasive tumor does not directly involve the inked transection line.
C. Evaluate the presence and tier of tumor budding exclusively using standard hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining.
D. Utilize cytokeratin immunohistochemistry (IHC) to confirm and accurately quantify the ambiguous cells at the advancing edge.
E. Upstage the lesion to Stage III (N1c) due to the presence of intermediate-to-high tier tumor budding.
F. Conclude that the polyp is non-malignant because the depth of submucosal invasion is less than 1 mm.

**Answer:** B, D

**Rationale:**
The pathologic evaluation of endoscopically resected pT1 colorectal polyps (malignant polyps) requires meticulous assessment of multiple histologic features to risk-stratify patients and determine the need for subsequent surgical resection. Key components of this evaluation include margin status, depth of submucosal invasion, and the presence of adverse prognostic factors such as tumor budding. Current standardized pathology protocols emphasize precise definitions to guide clinical decision-making. Specifically, the definition of a positive margin has evolved to strictly mean tumor cells present directly on the inked transection line ("ink on tumor"). Furthermore, the assessment of tumor budding—a critical factor for predicting lymph node metastasis in pT1 tumors—has become highly standardized. While routine assessment can often be performed on standard hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) stains, modern international consensus guidelines advocate for the use of cytokeratin immunohistochemistry (IHC) to resolve ambiguous cases and reduce interobserver variability, ensuring accurate tiering and risk stratification.

Option B is correct because current standardized pathology reporting protocols (such as those from the College of American Pathologists) dictate that a margin is negative unless invasive carcinoma directly involves the inked transection line. A distance of 0.8 mm is formally classified as a negative margin, although it clinically constitutes a "close margin" (≤1 mm) which may still be considered an unfavorable risk feature for deciding on surgical management.

Option D is correct because modern consensus guidelines, including those from the International Tumor Budding Consensus Conference (ITBCC), recommend utilizing cytokeratin immunohistochemistry (IHC) when the evaluation of tumor budding on H&E is difficult or ambiguous. Cytokeratin IHC enhances the visibility of isolated tumor cells and small clusters (≤4 cells) at the invasive front, thereby significantly improving diagnostic accuracy and reproducibility among pathologists.

Option A is incorrect because it reflects an outdated or colloquial clinical definition of margin positivity. While historical literature and some older clinical guidelines grouped margins ≤1 mm as "positive" due to their similarly elevated risk of residual disease, contemporary pathologic staging protocols strictly reserve the term "positive margin" exclusively for tumor at the ink. Categorizing a 0.8 mm margin as positive misrepresents modern standardized pathologic criteria.

Option C is incorrect as it relies on an outdated methodology of interpreting tumor budding exclusively on H&E staining in all scenarios. While H&E remains the initial standard, restricting evaluation exclusively to H&E in the face of ambiguous morphology fails to leverage modern immunohistochemical tools that current guidelines formally recommend to mitigate interobserver variability.

Option E is incorrect because it fundamentally conflates tumor budding with tumor deposits. In the AJCC TNM staging system, the N1c category (which designates Stage III disease) is reserved specifically for tumor deposits—discrete nodules of cancer in the pericolic or perirectal fat without evidence of residual lymph node architecture. Tumor budding refers to microscopic cellular clusters at the advancing edge of the primary tumor and, despite being a high-risk prognostic feature, does not upstage a localized pT1 lesion to Stage III.

Option F is incorrect because the diagnosis of a malignant polyp is based on the anatomical layer of invasion, not the absolute depth. Any tumor invading through the muscularis mucosa into the submucosa constitutes a pT1 adenocarcinoma (a malignant polyp). A submucosal invasion depth of <1 mm is a recognized "favorable" histologic feature that may support endoscopic management alone in the absence of other risk factors, but it does not negate the fundamental malignancy of the lesion.

A 45-year-old asymptomatic Asian male with a known history of chronic hepatitis B virus infection, but no evidence of cirrhosis on prior imaging or laboratory evaluation, undergoes routine right upper quadrant ultrasound during a follow-up visit. The study reveals a 2.5 cm solitary liver mass. Further characterization with multiphasic MRI demonstrates intense arterial phase enhancement with marked washout in both the portal venous and delayed phases, findings highly suggestive of hepatocellular carcinoma. The patient has no prior history of liver malignancy and is otherwise in good health. He is referred to a hepatology specialist to determine the next appropriate diagnostic and management steps. Separately, a 62-year-old female with metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH) and biopsy-proven cirrhosis (Child-Pugh Class A) presents for routine surveillance. She is asymptomatic, has stable liver function tests, and no history of viral hepatitis. She has not undergone prior HCC screening. Additionally, a 28-year-old Caucasian male with a remote diagnosis of chronic hepatitis B infection (diagnosed five years ago during blood donation) presents for primary care evaluation. His current labs show normal liver enzymes, undetectable HBV DNA, normal platelet count, and a recent FibroScan indicating no liver fibrosis. He has no family history of hepatocellular carcinoma and is concerned about his personal risk and need for screening.

**Select all that apply:**
A. Apply LI-RADS criteria to confirm the diagnosis non-invasively in the 45-year-old patient with chronic hepatitis B and characteristic imaging findings
B. Perform a core needle biopsy of the liver mass in the 45-year-old patient to confirm histology before treatment
C. Initiate hepatocellular carcinoma screening with liver ultrasound and serum alpha-fetoprotein every 6 months in the 62-year-old female with MASH-related cirrhosis
D. Initiate hepatocellular carcinoma screening with liver ultrasound alone every 6 months in the 28-year-old male with chronic hepatitis B and no fibrosis
E. No hepatocellular carcinoma screening is currently indicated for the 28-year-old male with chronic hepatitis B, no fibrosis, and undetectable viral load
F. Recommend prophylactic antiviral therapy indefinitely without radiologic screening for the 45-year-old patient with chronic hepatitis B and a liver mass showing classic HCC imaging features

**Answer:** A, C, E

**Rationale:**
In the 45-year-old patient with chronic hepatitis B and a liver mass exhibiting arterial phase hyperenhancement and washout on multiphasic MRI, the imaging findings meet diagnostic criteria for hepatocellular carcinoma. Current guidelines from the American Association for the Study of Liver Diseases (AASLD) and the American College of Radiology (ACR) support the use of LI-RADS for non-invasive diagnosis of HCC in high-risk populations beyond just those with cirrhosis, including patients with chronic HBV infection. Given the high specificity of these imaging features in this at-risk group, biopsy is not required and carries risks such as tumor seeding or bleeding, making non-invasive diagnosis appropriate. Therefore, applying LI-RADS criteria (Option A) is a guideline-concordant approach. In contrast, performing a core needle biopsy (Option B) was historically more common when imaging criteria were considered valid only in cirrhotic livers, but this approach is now discouraged in favor of non-invasive diagnosis when imaging is diagnostic, as it delays treatment and introduces procedural risk. For the 62-year-old female with MASH-related cirrhosis, surveillance for HCC is strongly indicated regardless of etiology, as the annual risk exceeds 1.5% in cirrhotic patients. The combination of ultrasound and alpha-fetoprotein (Option C) is recommended by several major guidelines, including AASLD, because it improves detection sensitivity over ultrasound alone, particularly in obese patients or those with suboptimal imaging windows. While some international guidelines use ultrasound alone, the addition of AFP is considered standard in many U.S.-based practices to enhance early tumor detection. Initiating screening with ultrasound alone in the 28-year-old male (Option D) is not appropriate because he does not meet current risk stratification criteria for HCC screening. Patients with chronic HBV require individualized assessment, and screening is reserved for higher-risk subgroups, such as those with cirrhosis, elevated viral load, family history of HCC, or specific demographic-risk profiles (e.g., Asian males over 40). This patient has no fibrosis, undetectable HBV DNA, and no additional risk factors, placing his annual HCC risk well below the threshold for cost-effective screening. Thus, no screening is currently indicated (Option E), which aligns with contemporary risk-adapted strategies. Recommending indefinite antiviral therapy without imaging (Option F) is incorrect in the context of a suspicious liver mass with diagnostic imaging features. While antiviral therapy is indicated for chronic HBV, it does not replace the need for HCC diagnosis and management. In a patient with a lesion meeting diagnostic criteria for HCC, deferring imaging-based diagnosis in favor of medical therapy alone would delay potentially curative treatment and is not supported by guidelines.

A 62-year-old male with metastatic clear cell renal cell carcinoma presents with mild cognitive slowing and intermittent headaches. Brain MRI demonstrates six discrete parenchymal metastases, each less than 1.5 cm in diameter, distributed across both cerebral hemispheres. His extracranial disease is stable on systemic therapy, and he maintains an ECOG performance status of 1. He has no evidence of leptomeningeal disease or significant cerebral edema. Given the number of intracranial lesions, the neuro-oncology team is considering radiation-based interventions to achieve durable intracranial control. The patient is neurologically functional and expresses strong concern about long-term cognitive side effects. A multidisciplinary discussion is underway to determine the optimal approach to his brain metastases. Additionally, a 38-year-old woman with a known germline fumarate hydratase (FH) mutation, diagnosed with hereditary leiomyomatosis and renal cell cancer (HLRCC), undergoes surveillance abdominal MRI, which reveals a 2.4 cm solid, exophytic mass in the lower pole of the left kidney. There is no venous invasion, lymphadenopathy, or distant metastasis. Her eGFR is 95 mL/min/1.73m², and she is highly motivated to preserve renal function. She is otherwise asymptomatic and in excellent health. Finally, a 45-year-old man with a familial FH mutation presents with weight loss, fatigue, and a persistent cough. Imaging shows a 7 cm right renal mass and multiple bilateral pulmonary nodules. A lung biopsy confirms metastatic HLRCC-associated renal cell carcinoma. The tumor board is convening to determine first-line systemic therapy.

**Select all that apply:**
A. Whole-brain radiation therapy (WBRT)
B. Stereotactic radiosurgery (SRS)
C. Radical nephrectomy
D. Partial nephrectomy
E. Erlotinib plus bevacizumab
F. Cabozantinib

**Answer:** B, C, E

**Rationale:**
For the patient with six brain metastases from clear cell renal cell carcinoma, stereotactic radiosurgery (SRS) is the preferred intervention despite the number of lesions. Contemporary evidence supports the use of SRS for patients with multiple brain metastases (up to 10 lesions) when lesions are small and well-demarcated, as in this case. SRS provides excellent local control while minimizing neurocognitive toxicity compared to whole-brain radiation therapy (WBRT), which is now reserved for patients with diffuse, non-targetable disease or those who cannot undergo focal therapy. The shift away from routine WBRT is driven by long-term neurocognitive preservation and comparable survival outcomes in patients treated with SRS, even with multiple metastases.

Whole-brain radiation therapy (WBRT) is no longer recommended as first-line treatment for patients with multiple but limited brain metastases due to its significant neurocognitive sequelae, including memory decline and reduced quality of life. While historically used for multiple lesions, modern guidelines restrict WBRT to cases of extensive intracranial disease burden where SRS is impractical. In this patient with only six small, discrete metastases and good performance status, WBRT would expose him to unnecessary toxicity without survival benefit, making it an outdated approach.

Radical nephrectomy is the standard surgical management for renal tumors in patients with HLRCC, regardless of tumor size. These tumors are highly aggressive and exhibit early metastatic potential, even when small. Nephron-sparing approaches such as partial nephrectomy are associated with higher local recurrence rates and are not recommended due to oncologic risk. Complete surgical extirpation via radical nephrectomy is necessary to achieve adequate cancer control in this genetic syndrome.

Partial nephrectomy, while ideal for many small renal masses in sporadic or less aggressive hereditary syndromes, is contraindicated in HLRCC due to the aggressive biology of the tumor. Even a 2.4 cm lesion in this context carries high metastatic risk, and attempts at parenchymal-sparing surgery may result in positive margins or residual disease. Preserving renal function is important, but not at the expense of oncologic safety in this high-risk population.

Erlotinib plus bevacizumab is the recommended first-line systemic therapy for metastatic HLRCC-associated renal cell carcinoma. This combination targets the unique molecular features of FH-deficient tumors, including upregulation of hypoxia-inducible factors and EGFR pathways. Clinical trials have demonstrated improved response rates and progression-free survival with this regimen compared to standard VEGF-targeted therapies used in clear cell RCC, making it the preferred option for this distinct subtype.
